#8789. The Science of “Extreme” Exercise During Pregnancy

The author attended the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto to hear directly from Margie Davenport and Michelle Mottola, key researchers shaping the upcoming 2027 International Olympic Committee guidelines. The resulting piece analyzes their latest clinical and survey data on pregnant athletes engaging in heavy weightlifting, high-intensity intervals, endurance sports, and rock climbing.

Back in 2019, I wrote about a new set of guidelines for exercise during pregnancy. These guidelines were revolutionary—up to a point. Advice from doctors at the time was often extremely conservative, like never letting your heart rate exceed 140 beats per minute. But solid evidence now suggested that consistent moderate exercise—at least 150 minutes spread over at least three days per week—was not just safe for most pregnant women but was actually beneficial for both mother and fetus, dramatically lowering the risk of conditions such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and depression.

Sign up for a ten-part email series from Alex Hutchinson on how to train, fuel, and recover. Each week, Alex covers a new topic, including strength training, supplements, and more!

Beyond that threshold, though, the deadlines dared not tread. Moderate exercise? Sure. Lifting heavy weights, or running marathons, or going rock climbing? That’s a trickier question, because no scientist wants to send a pregnant person out to do something that could potentially harm her or her baby. But ignoring it doesn’t make sense, because many female athletes do continue participating in their sports while pregnant, regardless of what the guidelines say. And those who stop or dramatically reduce their activity may suffer declines in both physical and mental health.

It’s important, then, to understand what the evidence says about the risks and benefits of more extreme forms of exercise. In 2018, the answer was “not much.” But in the years since then, there has been a steady flow of research on pregnant athletes doing hard things. In fact, the International Olympic Committee is planning to release a new and dramatically revised set of guidelines for pregnant athletes in 2027.

At the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto last week, I had a chance to hear two key authors of both the old and new guidelines—Margie Davenport of the University of Alberta and Michelle Mottola of Western University—speak about their research. They couldn’t yet reveal what’s in the new guidelines, but they did share some of the key research that informs them. Here are some highlights from the extreme frontiers of exercise and pregnancy.

Any sort of heavy lifting is frowned upon during pregnancy, and particularly lifting while lying on your back, which could compress key blood vessels. But this advice, Davenport points out, is based on expert opinion and workplace studies, where heavy lifting is different from lifting in the gym where you control load and recovery.

To start, she and her colleagues surveyed 679 recreational weightlifters and CrossFit athletes who were pregnant and habitually lifted at least 80 percent of their one-rep max. Those who continued heavy lifting had a 51 percent reduction in complications compared to those who obeyed the guidelines and dialed back their training. They were also roughly half as likely as normal to report postpartum depression after delivery.

Of course, survey studies have limitations: maybe complications caused people to stop lifting rather than the other way around, for example. But those initial positive results paved the way for bringing 10 pregnant women into the lab and having them do squats, bench press, and deadlift for 10 reps at up to 90 percent of 10-rep max. They monitored maternal and fetal heart rate, umbilical blood pressure, glucose and lactate levels, and various other health markers, and compared the results to those of ten non-pregnant controls; there were no causes for concern.

A heart-rate limit of 140 is outdated. Still, the 2019 guidelines remain cautious. “Vigorous” exercise, they suggest, should top out at around 169 beats per minute for women 29 and younger, and 162 beats per minute for those 30 and older.

In a 2023 study, Davenport and her colleagues put that ceiling to the test. They had 15 volunteers, at an average of 27 weeks pregnant, do either a 30-minute moderate bike ride or 10 x 1:00 intervals at above 90 percent of their predicted maximum heart rate. The women ended up reaching a peak of 96 percent on average during the intervals, with some getting as high as 105 percent of max. (This isn’t Spinal Tap: the standard estimate of max heart rate, 220 minus age, was clearly off for these women.)

Once again, the researchers took a bunch of measures of fetal and maternal physiological responses. There were no relevant differences between the moderate and intense exercise sessions.

This was another survey study: 331 women who, on average, were 33.2 years old and had completed 2.1 pregnancies. All had engaged in exercise bouts lasting at least an hour during their pregnancies; 80 percent had continued long-duration exercise throughout their pregnancies, but in most cases had gradually decreased overall training as the pregnancy progressed.

Davenport and her colleagues divided the respondents into two subgroups: those who continued to do at least 300 minutes of exercise per week during their third trimester, and those who were below that threshold. Those in the high exercise group had a lower risk of complications during delivery, but a higher risk of diastasis recti—a separation of the stomach muscles—after delivery.

The overall conclusion was that long-duration exercise well above guideline recommendations “appears to be well tolerated” by people who are already used to that level of training.

Here’s where things get interesting, because it’s hard to wave away the hypothetical dangers of a hard fall. But do these risks justify telling people not to climb?

Davenport has led a couple of studies exploring this issue. One involved interviewing 11 elite climbers who continued to train or compete during pregnancy about their perspectives on risk. Climbing, one of the climbers said, was actually safer than walking down the street: “I’m less likely to fall because I’ve got three points of contact on, compared to one when I’m walking… So I feel like I’m more likely to trip over something in the dark on the street than falling while climbing up a climbing wall.”

The second study surveyed nearly 700 climbers who had climbed through pregnancy, logging a cumulative total of 64,000 hours of climbing and suffering 155 self-diagnosed “hard falls.” Here there were two adverse events (one vaginal bleeding, the other undeclared), but both births were healthy. Climbing isn’t without risks, Davenport says, but the findings suggest the risks are lower than previously thought. Of note, 96 percent of respondents were “happy” or “very happy” they had continued to climb.

There’s more—Davenport has also studied contact sports like soccer, for example—but you get the picture. Some of these activities clearly involve theoretical risks, but those theoretical risks need to be balanced against the measurable mental and physical benefits of continuing to train and the risks of stopping. One of the best predictors of post-pregnancy injury, for example, is having reduced your training by more than 50 percent during pregnancy.

The focus of the upcoming IOC guidelines will be “athlete-centered decision-making”—not an ironclad set of rules about who can do which types of exercise when, but a framework about how to weigh the pros and cons in different contexts. It’s an important update, because it recognizes what’s already happening in the real world. “Our current public health guidance is fantastic and sets our baseline,” Davenport says. “But most athletes—well, all athletes—are going to vastly exceed current recommendations.”

For more Sweat Science, sign up for the email newsletter and check out my new book The Explorer’s Gene: Why We Seek Big Challenges, New Flavors, and the Blank Spots on the Map.

#8788. Stop Cramming Bikes in Your Car. These 10 Editor-Tested Hitch Racks Make Hauling Easier and More Secure

Our editors hauled bikes for thousands of miles to find the easiest, sturdiest hitch racks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cramming your bike into your car or SUV gets old quickly. Removing wheels and getting mud or grease all over your interior is no fun, and transporting your bike inside your car also leaves less room for passengers, luggage, or gear. Hitch-mount racks are the easiest, most secure way to carry your bike to your riding destination without mess or hassle. They’re ideal for heading to your local mountain bike trails, taking a road trip with friends, or going for weekend rides with your kids.

Hitch racks mount to the receiver on your vehicle’s bumper, making hitch racks easier to load than roof racks—hoisting a heavy bike onto an SUV’s roof after a long ride is never fun. Plus, you don’t need to remove your front wheel. Unlike roof racks, you can also drive into parking garages and drive-thrus with bikes on a hitch rack. And importantly, in an era of sky-high fuel prices, hitch racks typically impact your gas mileage less than roof-mounted options.

While hitch racks usually cost more than simple, low-cost trunk-mount racks, they can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. Hitch-mount carriers can also carry heavier bikes, like electric bikes or full suspension rigs, than trunk racks and are more stable at highway speeds.

Our editors and test team evaluated dozens of hitch racks to see which ones perform best. Our staff has used some of these racks on their own vehicles for years, safely transporting bikes over tens of thousands of miles. Our picks for the best hitch-mounted bike racks vary in features like position, trunk access functionality, bike capacity, and price—but all are dependable options for your next cycling trip.

Based on price, weight capacity, and ease of use, Thule’s Outpace ranks as our current Best Overall pick. The Outpace is lighter and more compact than most hitch racks, which makes it easy to install and remove. At only 28 pounds, it’s light enough to carry across the garage and slide into the receiver tube. Setup takes less than a minute, so you can mount it on the car when you need to haul your bikes (rather than it semi-permanently living on your bumper).

The rack can accommodate a wider range of bike wheel sizes, making it great for families. The rack adapts easily to any size bicycle in either position. The tradeoff for this versatility is that it takes a bit longer to load than bulkier racks with cinch-style clamps. But for something that can carry all of our bikes, and is so quick to install or remove that it never has to be a permanent fixture, that’s a small price to pay.

Our tester noted the Outpace’s receiver arm is on the short side. It fit snugly against the bumper with about two inches to spare, but on another vehicle, it wouldn’t fit without a hitch extender.

The Trail Rider is a great, lower-cost alternative to premium racks. It holds two bikes in fixed wheel mounts, secured with a single ratcheting arm that clamps down over the frame. The upright beam (which holds the frame holders) folds back and out of the way for trunk access; it’s also handy for loading up two bikes. We could fold it down, set a bike on the rack closest to the car without lifting it up and over the arm, then lift the arm back into place and position the second bike.

The trade-off for the Trail Rider’s low price isn’t stability or strength, but adjustability: The bikes are positioned in a fixed location. You have limited ability to separate them if two bikes don’t fit well together. That said, you can stagger the wheel cradles so the bars and saddles don’t interfere.

The Swagman XTC2 is one of the most affordable 2-bike racks we recommend. This no-frills rack is a solid choice for budget-conscious riders. It fits both 1¼-inch and 2-inch receiver tubes, and it accommodates wheel sizes from 20 to 29 inches. However, with a total weight capacity of 70 pounds (35 pounds per bike), it’s not suitable for e-bikes.

As expected at this price, the rack has some trade-offs. The wheel hoops are adjustable, but not as smoothly or precisely as on more premium racks. The rack doesn’t tilt away from the vehicle when loaded, limiting access to tailgates or liftgates. Lastly, you must remove the center support bar to load a bike on the inside tray.

Yet, the XTC2 is lightweight, durable, and very reasonably priced. If you’re willing to trade a bit of convenience for significant savings, the Swagman XTC2 is a reliable and practical option.

The Piston Pro X is our runner-up for Best Overall hitch rack; its construction, features, and style make it a standout pick in the category. Aside from the high price, the Piston Pro X is almost the perfect hitch rack for most users.

With the Piston Pro X, Küat elevated the rack from something purely utilitarian to a desirable piece of gear that’s easier to use than other racks. The rack includes smart features (such as integrated brake and turn-signal lights) and can carry more wheel sizes (and more weight) than almost any other rack on the market.

The top-end Pro X model costs more than almost any other hitch-mount rack, but it has proven extremely durable and maintains its good looks. It's also available in 3- and 4-bike models. Küat also offers a slightly cheaper Piston Pro variant, which ditches the Kashima coating on the pistons and the integrated brake lights and turn signals.

If you like the Küat racks but $1,600 is out of your price range, the brand offers several other hitch-style racks that could meet your needs. One great option is the Sherpa 2.0 model.

While the Sherpa doesn’t have the features or carrying capacity of Küat’s more expensive racks, it has two big upsides—color options and low weight. The Sherpa weighs only 32 pounds (claimed) in the 2-inch hitch configuration (1.25-in. also available). Küat offers the Sherpa in three colors: black metallic (with a silver accent), grey metallic (with orange), and pearl white (with silver).

The Sherpa carries two bicycles weighing up to 40 pounds per tray. So it’s ideal for non-electric road, gravel, and mountain bikes. It has an integrated cable lock to secure your bikes during rest stops or meal breaks, and it features a foot-operated lever to lower the rack into position for loading bikes.

It’s often difficult to carry e-bikes that are equipped with racks and fenders on traditional hitch racks. That’s because many hitch racks secure the bike with extending arms that clamp one or both wheels. However, Thule’s EasyFold XT model holds your bike by its frame.

Another feature that makes the EasyFold ideal for e-bike owners is the included ramp. This makes loading or removing your bikes much easier; no more wrestling with heavy bikes or front wheels or handlebars flopping as you load them onto the rack. And the ramp attaches to the rack when you’re finished.

Thanks to the rack’s 45-pound weight, it’s easy to remove it from your vehicle when you’re not using it. It folds down and features casters (which make moving it around your garage easier). The EasyFold XT’s biggest drawback is that Thule only rates it to 65 pounds per bike. While that will accommodate many e-bikes, some fat tire models may weigh too much.

When Thule debuted the T2 over a decade ago, it raised the bar for what cyclists expect from a hitch-mounted bike rack. Over the years, Thule updated the rack to accommodate wider tires and different wheel sizes. It also improved the T2’s look and made it easier to operate. One of the best recent upgrades is a wide-trigger handle that allows you to raise and lower the rack (and dip it out of the way for access to rear hatches) with one hand.

Integrated cable locks help keep your bikes secure for quick stops, and each tray can hold a bicycle up to 60 pounds and tires up to 5 inches wide. This makes the T2 a good option for all but the heaviest e-bikes. The T2 Pro’s arms have wide, comfortable grips that slide easily to secure the front wheel. Instead of using a bolt, the rack secures to your hitch receiver with an expansion wedge that tightens with a locking knob. The system makes installing and removing the T2 easier (though it weighs 52 pounds), but it’s not foolproof.

Yakima’s StageTwo two-bike rack goes head-to-head with premium offerings from Küat and Thule at a lower price. In about 2,500 miles of on-car testing, the StageTwo impressed us with its ease of use and flex-free performance. This rack is only rated up to 35 pounds per tray, so it’s not made for transporting e-bikes. However, it’s one of only two racks on this list that accommodates wheels as small as 16 inches.

The StageTwo’s trays are offset, which means less chance of contact when carrying two similarly sized bikes (however, bikes sit more widely apart, so watch those tight parking spaces). The rack includes two SKS locking cables (they don’t auto-retract, so tuck them back in when not in use). The StageTwo also includes an integrated lock loop for extra security when parked or locking your rack off the vehicle.

The rack is offered in 1.25- and 2-inch sizes. The 2-inch variant can accommodate four bikes with an add-on kit. Also, check Yakima’s fit guide before buying—One of our testers experienced a hardware fitment issue.

If you travel to mountain resort towns (or have been around trailheads or bike parks lately), you’ve probably seen behemoth racks like these on the back of vans and trucks. Since modern mountain bikes are bulky, racks like Thule’s ReVert make sense if you’re hauling a full load with a single vehicle.

The ReVert holds six bikes, loads quickly, and sticks out no farther than a standard 2-bike horizontal rack. Its carrying capacity makes it ideal for large families, race teams, or ride groups.

At over 87 pounds, the ReVert is undeniably heavy. However, a few smart features make the rack manageable. Dual hydraulic dampers assist with lowering the rack when it’s fully loaded, so you don’t have to wrestle with it. Once in the lowered position, even shorter riders and kids can lift their bikes high enough to slot them into the baskets. Individual bikes are spaced 11 inches apart, giving you plenty of room to carry any combination—flat bar, drop bar, even cruisers.

1UP USA has built a cult-like following with its industrial-looking racks that take a simplistic approach to securing your bike. This model features two ratcheting arms that clamp down on your wheels—no hooks or straps necessary.

The Equip-D’s pivot mechanism is smooth and reliable even after years of abuse (although an occasional shot of WD-40 White Lithium Grease Spray goes a long way in keeping the release mechanism running smoothly). A T-handle release positioned at the end of the hitch bar means you don’t need to reach through the rack to fold it up. Tiered trays position bikes closer together, and the rack rides out of the way of most exhaust pipes. 1Up also offers the Equip in a single-bike version for a sleeker look.

Hitch racks are bicycle carriers that attach to your vehicle’s hitch receiver. Popular models carry one to four bikes, but some hanging-style hitch racks can haul up to six bikes.

A hitch is a standard feature on most trucks and many SUVs. However, if you have a car or wagon, a hitch can often be added. If your vehicle doesn’t already have a receiver, it’s easy to have one installed. (U-Haul is a reliable and affordable option for installation.)Receivers come in two sizes: 1¼-inch and 2-inch (measured across the inside of the square opening). Most trucks and SUVs use a 2-inch receiver. Many racks are available in both sizes, but heavier-duty racks—and racks that carry three or more bikes—often require the larger 2-inch receiver for added strength and stability. Racks rated to carry heavyweight e-bikes also typically require a 2-inch receiver.

If the rack will live on your vehicle year-round or see frequent use, invest in the most durable model your budget allows. While all racks listed here secure bikes effectively, higher-priced options tend to have sturdier moving parts—ratchets, straps, buckles, and locks—that stand up better to long-term use.

Not all hitch racks are rated for the extra weight of e-bikes. Those that aren’t suited for heavier bikes are clearly noted in our reviews.

Some racks are quite heavy, which contributes to their strength but can be inconvenient if you plan to remove and reinstall the rack frequently.

For most vehicles—aside from sedans—accessing the trunk or tailgate is restricted when the rack is in use or folded up. Many of our top picks offer tilt-down designs that allow you to open the back of your vehicle even with bikes loaded. For full access, swing-away adapters like the Küat Pivot v2 Swing-Away allow the entire rack to pivot 90 degrees, completely clearing the rear of your car or truck.

Need more clearance? Sometimes a simple hitch extender can do the trick. For added stability and peace of mind, we also recommend using an anti-rattle clamp with any rack you choose.

Pros: Hitch racks strike the perfect balance between the ease of access of a trunk rack and the security of a quality roof rack. They slot into your car’s hitch receiver, relying on no flimsy straps or sketchy hooks. They’re also positioned behind your car, which is great for gas mileage and roof-collision prevention (low standing height). Better yet, many are modular, allowing you to add extra trays, locks, and even bottle openers for more personalized functionality.

Cons: These racks are the most consistently expensive out there—quality materials and a confidence-inspiring construction unquestionably affect their price. Furthermore, they can be a pain to remove, as most options weigh well over 40 pounds and need tools to detach. Furthermore, with bikes on the rack, they add significant length to your vehicle, which could prove tricky if you need to parallel park. And most critically, not every car has a hitch, which means you’ll either need to install one yourself or forego this style entirely.

Our editors drove hundreds (and in some cases, thousands) of miles with their bikes on these racks. We hauled road bikes, mountain bikes, e-bikes, and city bikes. We carried bikes with disc brakes, big wheels, and fat tires. Our test team used these racks for months, in various environments and conditions. We tested them in the salty winters of Pennsylvania, the high mountains of Colorado, and the gritty Arizona desert.

#8785. I Wish Yoga Studios Would Stop Trying to Sell Me on Their Teacher Training Programs

Los Angeles-based yoga instructor Ramoni Overton questions whether a common trend across yoga studios is negatively affecting students. Overton is the creator of the YouTube channel Yoga With Ramoni.

I was brand new to yoga when I first experienced a teacher training sales pitch at the end of class. I had stood up after Savasana feeling pure bliss, practically floating off my mat. But suddenly the instructor was pedaling the studio’s upcoming yoga teacher training (YTT) to the entire room. I was surprised, but I mostly brushed it off, assuming it was a one-time thing.

But then it happened a second time. Then a third. And a fifth. After I heard the exact same sales pitch multiple times, my post-class high vanished before I even made it to the front door. It was replaced by a single thought. “Seriously? Again?”

This experience isn’t unique to me—it’s been happening to many other yoga students. And, in my opinion, it’s a reason why some of them might quietly not return to class.

As a yoga teacher for four years and a yoga student for nine, I’ve noticed that most students aren’t coming to yoga to build a second career. They already have full days and packed schedules. They’re coming to yoga to unwind, decompress, and experience a single hour in which the outside world completely disappears.

At the same time, I understand the reasons behind the post-class YTT pitch. Yoga studios have bills to pay, and YTT is one of the more reliable revenue streams in a business that runs on thin margins. But when studios push their instructors to pitch constantly (and when some instructors receive commission for every sign-up), the pressure is on. The yoga teacher who was supposed to hold space for you is now knowingly or unknowingly working a sales quota. That changes the energy of a studio, whether anyone admits it or not.

And it adds up to something that’s bigger than one annoying moment. Seemingly everywhere else in life, we are constantly being sold something. Ads interrupt us while we’re watching TV, listening to podcasts or the radio, and scrolling through social media. Yoga was supposed to be one of the few places that wasn’t also a marketing funnel.

Studios don’t need to stop sharing information about their YTT offerings. But they do need to stop treating every student on the mat as a sales lead. There are so many ways to share training info without disrupting the post-class quiet. A simple flyer at the front desk, an announcement on the studio schedule, or a free information session for those who are genuinely curious. Let people come, flow, and leave in peace.

If the training is enticing, students will ask about it on their own. You won’t have to sell them on it.

#8783. That Mysterious Bike Creak Is Driving You Crazy—Here’s How to Check Your Bottom Bracket

Simple checks to pinpoint bottom bracket creaks before they become bigger repairs.

As cyclists, we hear a lot of sounds when riding. Usually, the noises come from chirping birds, the wind rustling leaves, or your bike’s tires rolling over your favorite trail. But sometimes the noises sound bad and come from your bike, and those noises can range from annoying to anxiety-inducing as you ponder the cause.

Bicycle components are moving parts that wear out and sometimes need adjustment. These squeaks, creaks, clicks, and other strange sounds are often a sign that something on your bike needs repair or replacement. And if your bike seems extra noisy, it might be time for some routine maintenance.

Noises on bikes are sometimes frustrating and mysterious. It’s often a challenge to figure out exactly where the sound originates—especially if it’s hard to reproduce when not riding. When I ran a shop, we would have customers come in and they would be certain that a noise was coming from one spot—only to find the culprit be somewhere else. Many times a noise would originate at the cranks or bottom bracket, so that’s what we’ll focus on here.

It’s worth checking on the lowest hanging fruit before we dig into the bottom bracket. The most common noisemakers are loose parts or bearings requiring adjustment, cleaning, or replacement. Performing regular preride bolt checks helps keep components tight and noises at bay. Several spots on your bike use bearings to rotate smoothly, including your headset, bottom bracket, hubs, and suspension linkages on mountain bikes. Keep these bearings properly adjusted to cut down on squeaks and knocking sounds.

Before checking if the noise originates from your bottom bracket, check that the crank bolts (which affix the crank arms to the BB on many bikes) are sufficiently tight. You might hear a clicking when these bolts loosen. And if a crank bolt entirely backs out, it can cause a crankarm to fall off while riding or damage your crank or frame. Grab a torque wrench and tighten the bolts to the manufacturer’s recommended specification.

After you are sure the noise is not from a loose crankarm, stand next to your bike and grab both brakes. Then, put your foot on the pedal closest to you and press inward. If the bike still creaks or ticks when you put weight on the pedal, the problem likely comes from your bottom bracket.

If the clicking sound isn’t from your drivetrain or pedals (see below), your BB may be loose, or the bearings may be worn. Many bikes use a non-adjustable cartridge or press-fit BB that must be replaced when the bearings wear out. Some systems (such as SRAM DUB and Race Face Cinch) use a preload ring to add preload to the bottom bracket bearings. These rings can loosen and cause a click while pedaling. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to tighten it back up.

If you don’t hear anything, the problem is likely the bearings in your headset, hubs, or suspension parts. Bearings can wear out after a season, especially if you live somewhere wet or sandy. Your local bike shop can help you order and install new ones.

It’s also possible you simply need a new bottom bracket in the bike. Bottom bracket standards are a deep rabbit hole and can feel overly complex if you aren’t familiar with the system. Different frames and different cranks require different bottom brackets. Before searching Amazon for the best deal on bottom brackets, consult the technical specifications for your specific bike and component group or visit your local shop for direction.

I have seen bottom bracket issues actually cause issues on carbon frames as well. I’ve seen this specifically on older carbon frames with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained over time. All the bikes that I saw frame issues from bottom brackets fell into the same category: older carbon road bikes with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained for years. Eventually the customer would hear a noise, but keep riding. Then that noise would turn into knocking in the crank. By the time they got to our shop, the space in the frame for the bottom bracket was no longer a perfect circle. That circle shifted into an oval over time—which more times than not resulted in a new frame being needed. If you have a creak in your bottom bracket, get it checked out (or inspect it yourself) before it becomes something bigger.

#8782. Triathlon News, October 2026: Ironman Crashes, NYC Tri Returns, Middle East Racing

Tim Heming highlights the biggest news in triathlon in October 2026. (Photo: Triathlete)

In October, the triathlon world turned its eyes to the Big Island for another epic edition of the Ironman World Championship, but that didn’t stop the rest of the multisport world from serving up its usual mix of drama, debate, and headline-grabbing news.

From analyzing the sparse participation numbers at New York’s long-awaited race return to tackling safety, transparency, and course caps following a scary collision on the Queen K, October delivered plenty of food for thought. And, as always, contributor Tim Heming is here to digest it with you.

The first line of Sarah Wassner Flynn’s article about the return of the iconic New York City Triathlon, published earlier this year, reads: “For more than two decades, the New York City Triathlon was one of the sport’s most iconic races. Debuting in 2001, it quickly became a bucket-list event for age-groupers and pros alike.”

The piece previewed this year’s race return, renamed the Big Apple Triathlon, under new ownership of Alpha Win, formerly known as HITS Endurance, with Tommy Struzzieri taking over the company from his father, Tom.

Alpha Win, based in Saugerties, New York, is no novice when it comes to race hosting. They have put on over 200 races, but making a success of this one offered the sternest test of their credentials to date.

Held on October 10, the day when most eyes in the triathlon world were focused almost 5,000 miles west on the Big Island of Hawaii, would it prove enough of a draw to justify the set-up costs of a swim in the Hudson River, a bike up the closed West Side Highway, and a run through Central Park?

Since its halcyon days, the event has been beset by problems, with participation tumbling from a peak of almost 4,000 during its time as part of the Life Time Fitness Series in 2010. In 2024, it was canceled by new owner Supertri before registration even opened, with organizers saying they couldn’t find a suitable date. It didn’t return in 2025 either, which, given Supertri’s focus on producing stylish, short-course events in major urban areas, had to be a worrying sign.

“We’re just trying to bring back something that athletes have been asking for,” Struzzieri said in March, noting that numbers would be capped at 2,500. If that felt optimistic, a New York Post piece on the eve of the event recounted its troubled history and asked: Is this time the charm? stating that around 1,300 athletes were expected to start, with prices ranging from $350–$650.

The results, however, show fewer than half that number: only around 600 finishers across all formats, the lowest the event has seen since it began in 2001. “Every year that there’s an issue with this event, it hurts the event the following year,” Scott Nilson, Supertri’s U.S. general manager of events, told us in 2024. Perhaps this year it will be the simple economics of numbers.

Registration for the 2027 event is now open with early-bird pricing (including processing fees) at $548.90 (Olympic distance) and $383.90 (sprint distance). Triathlete reached out to Alpha Win for comment.

For the majority, the Ironman World Championship is a day of celebration and achievement. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience, the ultimate triathlon dream. For Trish Byron, that dream turned into a nightmare.

Byron was struck by a male cyclist from behind almost 30 miles into the bike leg, leaving her with seven fractured ribs, a broken collarbone, a punctured and partially collapsed lung, a concussion, a laceration requiring stitches, and extensive road rash.

It’s understood the cyclist stopped and spoke with volunteers before continuing the race, but Byron’s daughter Cassie Anne put out a plea on Facebook for more information, saying: “We’re hoping to gather firsthand accounts, identify the cyclist involved, and better understand what happened.”

Accidents happen, but the incident raises questions about transparency when serious collisions occur during races. Should such incidents be publicly reported, both to demonstrate that appropriate safety protocols and follow-up procedures have been followed and to help triathletes better understand the risks involved in signing up?

Cassie Anne’s post received a response from Judy Daggett, who said: “This exact scenario happened to me on the bike about mile 85, causing me to crash also. The guy who hit me kept going. Another athlete helped me to my feet.

“I immediately had double vision and said, ‘Yes, I need help,’ but there was no one around. I managed to get back on the bike and ride to T2, praying my vision didn’t completely leave.

“When I got there, they took me by ambulance to the ER for a CT of my head, thinking I could possibly have a brain bleed. Thankfully, I did not, but I also have fractured ribs, a hip and shoulder injury, and a concussion.”

Daggett went on to say she’d reached out to Ironman but was yet to hear from them, stating it was her first DNF in 30 years and that the “men were so aggressive, they need to let them go first”.

Her final point relates to the questions raised about the scheduled swim start waves that interspersed the men’s and women’s age-group divisions in Hawaii, whereas previously, the men had been started earlier in one cohort, followed by the women.

It also brings into focus the broader question (that has continued to surface since the announcement of the return to one day of racing) of whether Ironman should cap numbers on the course for both fairness and safety reasons.

While it might seem that Trish Byron’s family shouldn’t have far to go to find answers, as Anna Grosz, who also responded to the post, explained, it might not be that simple: “I provided medical support for the race. We are bound by patient confidentiality laws. You should reach out to Ironman through official channels. The medical director may be able to communicate directly with the affected athlete, but course volunteers cannot do so.”

Triathlete has contacted Ironman for comment.

Championship season is not quite over in the world of triathlon. The T100 Tour still has three events on the calendar, with Dubai and Saudi Arabia in November ahead of the T100 World Championship Final in Qatar. The action in the Middle East will also continue with the 2026 World Triathlon Multisport Championship in Abu Dhabi.

The headlines will be the professional races over 100K where Hayden Wilde looks to be the odds-on favorite to retain his title, and it’s wide open on the women’s side. But there is also shorter-distance racing and representative age-group competition throughout.

Despite conflict in the region and the cancelation, postponement or relocation of other major sporting events, particularly in Saudi Arabia, both World Triathlon and the Professional Triathletes Organization are, for now, proceeding as planned. That’s perhaps to be expected, with contingency decisions often left until the last possible moment. But if the events do go ahead, it will be interesting to see how much appetite international athletes have for traveling to the region.

Conversations around weight can be a sensitive topic: triggering to some, frustrating to others, and almost irrelevant to others. And Susan Kitchen’s article on why we shouldn’t be concerning ourselves with post-race weight gain will no doubt grab the attention of athletes who might have concerns about how they can be heavier after doing all that exercise.

While Kitchen spells out the reasons here (which, spoiler alert, can be perfectly natural as your body recovers), it also made me think that perhaps the concern shouldn’t be how much you weigh, but why, in the days following an incredible endurance feat, you’re not off celebrating somewhere, rather than hopping on the scale.

You may not find an answer as to which is better, but there is plenty we can learn from Jordan Blanco’s roundtable discussion with triathlon legends Flora Duffy and Jan Frodeno when it comes to their appreciation for the pinnacle events in our sport – including that the 2008 win in Beijing was Frodeno’s first-ever elite victory!

But if there is one takeaway, then it’s probably that following your heart is the first step, and the financial rewards will follow. Doing it the other way around might just be a little tougher.

What do we learn from the Kona bike mechanics recounting tales from the Big Island?

Number one: That most of us should probably invest a bit more time in understanding how to fix our own bikes.

Number two: That whatever daft mistake you’ve made, it won’t be the dumbest thing they’ve seen (one athlete rolled up with two front wheels and no back, another with two back wheels and no front).

Number three: If you do have a problem, get to the mechanics early (the day before race day was the busiest).

And number four: Have a little patience. “That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations,” Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic working out of Bike Works Kona, told Sara Stover. “Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

But while being a bike mechanic sounds like a thankless task, it has some upsides. The real kicker, featuring five carbon wheels and the town’s dump, is cleverly left until the final line.

Some charitable sporting endeavors fall flat while others just fly, and often there seems to be no logic as to which cause will capture the public mood.

Thankfully, for Ethan Hunger, the idea to complete a world-record number of super sprint triathlons within 24 hours to raise money for his local food bank in Bellingham, Washington, really took off.

If ever there was a classic case of nominative determinism, then this is it. Hunger v. Hunger actually started following the COVID pandemic, but as Travis Mundell found out, this year’s challenge was the most ambitious yet, helping push the initiative’s total fundraising beyond $1.2 million.

It’s life-affirming to see such dedication in action, not just from Hunger, but from the community that rolled out to support him, where putting all the proper procedures in place so the record could be ratified by Guinness reads as more grueling than all that swimming, biking, and running.

There’s probably not much more that needs adding to one of the most dramatic Ironman World Championship races in living memory. Having written a reaction piece on how the house (in this case, the Big Island) always wins versus the gambler, I’ve reflected more on how it just seems such a difficult race to get right. My first thought: If the pros can’t do it (see the DNF files here), what chance do the mere mortals have? Follow-up thought: Nobody racing here could ever be described as a mere mortal anyway.

#8780. Zipp’s Cheapest Carbon Wheelset Makes a Strong Case for Itself—But There’s One Catch

A major-brand carbon wheelset at a lower price, with a great warranty and one trade-off road riders should consider.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Zipp’s 404S replaces the 303S with a deeper 50mm rim for modern road riding. Zipp says the new profile saves about two watts over its predecessor. At $1,300 for the pair, the wheels bring a familiar name and a lifetime warranty to a price well below the brand’s flagship models.

I rode the 404S on my steel Ritchey Road Logic, logging roughly 800 miles over two months. They’re a totally fine, solid wheelset. They feel settled at speed without riding harshly, accelerate well once they’re rolling, and remain stable in gusty conditions. In other words, Zipp made a perfectly good wheelset that will likely come stock on many SRAM-equipped bikes.

On the road, the 404S fades into the background of your ride (in a good way). The wheels feel comfortable without feeling harsh. Get them up to speed, and they are reassuringly solid. In terms of crosswind performance, I’d rate them quite good. They aren’t quite on the level of something like a Roval Rapide CLX III (basically the gold standard for crosswind performance), but they still feel very stable even on a gusty day. Once I'm moving, they have the responsive feel I expect from a 50mm wheelset, whether I’m pedaling through a corner or getting back up to speed on a rolling road.

The weight shows up more on steep climbs or when accelerating out of a slow corner; these wheels don’t have the immediate, lively feel of lighter aero options. That doesn’t make them feel sluggish in normal riding; it’s just the clearest difference I noticed after riding lighter wheels.

Otherwise, I found little to separate the 404S from more expensive wheelsets with a similar rim depth. They do the basic job well: they feel stable in the wind, comfortable on imperfect roads, and once you’re up to speed, their weight disadvantage largely disappears.

The 404S uses a Tubeless Straight Side, or hookless, rim design. That means checking tire compatibility and pressure limits before you ride. Zipp recommends tires from 28 to 39mm, and says the wheels are optimized for 28–29mm tires for best aero performance, with a maximum pressure of 72.5 psi. Many riders might miss that if you run a 30 or 32mm road tire, the maximum pressure limit drops to 65 psi, according to ETRTO.

Those limits may not affect riders who already use wider tires at lower pressures. But I still see hookless as a miss for road wheels in 2026 for many reasons. Sure, a handful of high-profile issues in the pro peloton didn’t help, but neither did the steady drip of unease coming from inside the industry itself. While Zipp has stood behind the standard, I’d rather give the company credit for acknowledging that many riders (including me) would prefer a hooked option. instead of dealing with a relatively low max tire-pressure limit, consulting pressure charts, and reading tire-compatibility lists.

ENVE, arguably the biggest proponent of hookless road wheels, has already made this pivot. The brand's flagship racing models, the SES 4.5 and 6.7 Pro wheels, both feature a “mini hook.” This leaves only Zipp and Giant/Cadex sticking with hookless for now, and given my predictions earlier this year, I would guess both are at least considering their options.

At $1,300, the 404S sits between a few other 50mm carbon wheelsets. HUNT’s 50 Carbon Disc is listed at $1,249, with a 50mm rim, 22mm internal width, and a hooked tire interface. HUNT lists its weight at 1,464 grams, making it a close alternative for about $50 less, with a hooked rim.

Shimano’s Ultegra C50 is another 50mm option, listed at $1,570 for the pair. It has a hooked rim and a 21mm internal width, making it a little more expensive than the Zipp, with a narrower rim bed.

The harder comparison for Zipp is basically any wheel from Light Bicycle. Light Bicycle’s complete Airia wheel builds start at $1,144, and that base build is claimed to weigh 1,218 grams. The 55mm-deep test set weighed 1,101 grams without tape or valves, though that specific build cost about $1,407. So the tested Airias were slightly more expensive than the 404S, but they were 5mm deeper and dramatically lighter (also hooked).

That makes the 404S a reasonably priced option from a major brand, but the weight is hard to overlook when lighter and sometimes cheaper wheels are available at similar or lower prices. But the 404S does have one way it stands above its competition. It comes with a lifetime warranty that covers not just manufacturing defects but also damage from intended use. This will appeal to many riders who would rather have a dependable wheel than a slightly lighter one.

#8779. 4 Things You’re Doing in Yoga That Might Worsen Lower Back Discomfort

Monica Bright is a yoga teacher whose continuing education centered on injury mechanics and movement. She breaks down the common yoga mistakes that could be worsening lower back discomfort, and offers options for relief. You can also learn more about yoga poses for your lower back.

Lower back discomfort is one of the most common pain points among people worldwide. If you fall into that category and also do yoga, chances are you’ve expected the practice to bring you relief. But certain movements in yoga, and how you approach them, can sometimes have the opposite effect of the lower back release that you were hoping to achieve.

Learning to recognize what triggers tightness in your lower back can help you make more supportive choices on and off the mat. That way, you’re still working toward undoing your discomfort, but without accidentally worsening it.

Whether you’re in class or at home, or even moving throughout your everyday life, notice whether any of the following approaches to movement worsens your lower back sensitivity—and explore the following alternatives that might help relieve your discomfort.

Some people’s lower back strain is aggravated by moving too quickly. This is often the case with forward rounding. Think Seated Forward Bend or reaching down to pick something up off the floor. Moving slowly allows you to pay attention to the sensations in your body and ensures you’re not accidentally forcing yourself to move too far into a stretch and tweak your lower back.

What to try instead: Throughout your yoga practice, and even during your day, ask yourself, “How does it feel when I move more slowly?”

The “neutral” position of your spine that you commonly hear yoga teachers mention includes several curves, including one in the lumbar spine that is concave, meaning it curves inward. But many students have a tendency to round the lower back during certain poses, such as forward bends and Chair Pose, which can have the effect of flattening the lower spine and causing tension.

What to try instead: Maintaining that neutral spine can be more beneficial than “flattening” it for some students with a track record of stiffness and soreness in the lower back. That comes into play in several common yoga poses.

In Chair Pose, for instance, there is a tendency to draw the core toward the spine so much that it counteracts the natural curve in the lower back. Maintaining a neutral spine means keeping the length in your lower back rather than tucking the tailbone.

In Standing Forward Bend, keeping a neutral spine means being aware if you are rounding your lower back as you reach forward and, instead, hinging at your hips, perhaps bending your knees, and not being concerned with how far forward you fold.

However, some students find a greater sense of ease in the lower back by rounding forward. Ask yourself, “Does my lower back feel better, or worse, with rounded forward folds?”

If your lower back is sensitive, your yoga practice might look different from the person’s on the mat next to you—and that’s okay. The goal in yoga isn’t to push past discomfort, but to find the alignment in which your lower back feels good. And sometimes that means taking variations.

What to try instead: Explore variations of poses—some of which might include using props, such as blocks—to help support your movements. Take Happy Baby, for example. Drawing your knees toward your chest and holding the backs of your thighs might feel more supportive to some. When sitting in a forward bend, placing a blanket underneath the lowest part of your back to slightly elevate your hips and provide more room for your lower back might be your preferred version. Finding the movement options that feel tolerable for you can be enormously helpful while you’re learning to prioritize your lower back.

Stress, poor sleep, a sense of being overwhelmed, even anxiety surrounding practicing certain movements can put your body on high alert and cause your nervous system to brace for impact. This has the potential to turn up the volume on physical discomfort. Understanding how to downregulate your nervous system, on the other hand, can help your entire body relax.

What to try instead: You’re likely familiar with some of the practices that activate your parasympathetic nervous system, including resting in poses such as Child’s Pose, Legs Up the Wall, or Crocodile and practicing various pranayama (breathwork) techniques, including Box Breathing or simply lengthening your exhalations. Even slowing the pace of your practice and taking the variations that feel good to you are ways of signaling to your nervous system that you’re safe. Experiment with one or two calming exercises prior to your next yoga class or at-home practice.

Practicing with these ideas in mind will ultimately help you recognize how to support your body when practicing yoga. This doesn’t mean you need to have to have all of the answers. It simply, but it does means that you are present, aware, and listening to your own body’s signals.

#8775. This $16 Tool Can Save You Thousands of Dollars Across the Life Span of Your Bike

Catch chain wear early and you could save hundreds—or more—on drivetrain replacements.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I’ve checked in thousands of bikes for service, and I used to hear this line all the time: “I ride the bike a lot, but it’s in great shape. The shifting just jumps around a little.” Once I would get to the step of putting a chain checker on the chain, that $16 tool might tell the story of hundreds of dollars in upcoming repairs.

A chain checker was one of my most recommended service tools to customers when I ran a bike shop service department. The key is to make sure you are buying the correct one and understand how to use it. The chain checker most shops I worked in was the Park Tool CC2 —the chain checker with the swivel dial.

This option was great because it gave customers and service advisors an easy visual on the wear level of a chain. But the biggest reason my favorite chain checker isn’t this one is because it does not give a clear reading on certain SRAM chains. Read on to find out which chain checker I suggest, why it can save you thousands of dollars across the life span of your bike, and how to use this small tool.

When a chain gets stretched it can cause issues like slow shifting, unexpected chain jumps, and the chain can have a slipping feeling under power. Sometimes these issues can also be mistaken for cable tension being off in a derailleur, but you can easily check the chain stretch at home if you have this chain checker.

It is extremely difficult to tell how worn a drivetrain is with the naked eye. By checking how worn a chain is, you can tell what other parts will need to be replaced. My favorite chain checker is the Pedro’s Chain Checker because it is compatible with most chain makes and models. It also retails for only $16 and it is small enough to fit in almost anyone’s tool roll or kit.

Many shops will recommend replacing an 11, 12, or 13 speed chain when a chain checker reads over 50 percent worn. If the chain is over 75 percent worn that recommendation changes to replacing a chain and cassette or freewheel (gears on the back wheel) and replacing chain, cassette or freewheel, and chainrings or crank (gears in the front near the pedals) when it measures over 100 percent worn. Typically 10-speed chains and lower have a bigger tolerance to stretch, with singlespeeds having the biggest acceptable stretch.

Many times a customer would ask if the shop could just throw a new chain onto a drivetrain that is past that 100 percent mark. If you do this, the shifting can actually get worse because the wear pattern in the new chain no longer lines up with the wear pattern on the existing cassette and chainrings. An even worse case scenario of putting a new chain on a worn drivetrain is chain suck. This is when a worn chainring can get stuck to the chain from the bottom of the pedal stroke. Then the chain gets sucked up and jammed between the chainring and the frame—possibly leading to damage on the frame. Once a drivetrain has a certain level of wear replacing only one part of the system does not work.

The price for some higher-end cassettes can range anywhere from $400 to $660 from brands like Shimano and SRAM. I go by a three-strike rule with chains (spokes too, but that’s a different story). For my own bikes I typically get three chains out of each cassette.

If you are on top of chain wear with a chain checker, this could save you almost $2,000 in cassette costs alone when using high-end SRAM cassettes. Remember, this price doesn’t include labor or the cost of chainrings—which you’ll need to replace if you keep running the chain until it’s above that 100 percent wear mark.

Some higher-end chainrings, like the SRAM Red direct-mount chainring, can run up to almost $300 per ring. If someone runs the whole drivetrain into the ground, then a checkup for shifting issues can quickly turn into a thousand-dollar bill on a high end drivetrain. If you’re running Shimano 105 or SRAM Rival, then being on top of chain wear might not save you thousands as quickly as running the highest end group set. Rest assured, overtime you’ll get there too. The better news is that Pedro's chain checker is so easy to use.

Start by dropping the tooth with the number one above it into the chain. Once the number one tooth is dropped in, then drop the tooth with the number two above it into the chain. Finally, try to drop the third tooth (numbered with a three) into the chain. If this tooth doesn’t drop in through the links in the chain, then good news! Your chain is less than 50 percent worn. If it drops halfway through the chain that means your chain is about 75 percent worn. Finally, if the tooth numbered three on the chain checker drops all the way through the chain that means it is between 75 percent and 100 percent worn. Typically I suggest if you have 11, 12, or 13 speed chains around that 50 percent worn mark change the chain soon to keep the rest drivetrain alive as long as possible.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8774. The 67-Year-Old Who Raced Two Full Ironmans a Week Apart

Mary Mitchell won her age group in Kona and eight days later raced Ironman California, where she also won her age group. Here's how she did it. (Photo: Mary Mitchell, FinisherPix)

Fresh off a sixth-place finish at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, American professional triathlete Sam Long recently took to Instagram to ask his followers a question. Should he race Ironman Florida on November 7, or give himself another two weeks to recover and race Ironman Cozumel on November 22?

Long wants to secure his qualification for the 2027 Ironman World Championship early, but the question of how quickly to return to racing after Kona is a serious one. Among the responses to his post were plenty of suggestions that he take the extra recovery time and race Cozumel instead.

After all, Kona is no ordinary Ironman. Its combination of heat, humidity, unpredictable winds and exposed terrain takes a major physical toll, even on athletes who have spent their careers preparing for those conditions. Racing another Ironman just four weeks later is ambitious enough. What about racing one eight days later?

For 67-year-old Australian age-grouper Mary Mitchell, that was precisely the challenge.

On October 10, Mitchell won the women’s 65-69 age group at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, finishing in 13:11:46. Eight days later, she lined up at Ironman California in Sacramento, where she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, more than 90 minutes faster than her Kona performance.

And she won her age group again. Even more remarkably, her husband, Andrew, 66, who had also raced in Kona, joined her in Sacramento and won his age group too.

What began as a somewhat improbable endurance experiment ended with three age-group victories between them.

The idea wasn’t actually Mary’s. Earlier this year, Mary and Andrew traveled to Morocco to spend time altitude training in the Atlas Mountains with a friend. During the trip, their friend floated an intriguing challenge. What would happen if a bunch of athletes in their 60s attempted two full-distance Ironmans a week apart?

“He persuaded us that it would be a good human experiment to do, to see whether, at our age, you could do two Ironmans in eight days, and what would that be like?” Mitchell explains.

The plan was for all three to qualify for Kona, race the World Championship, and then travel to Sacramento for Ironman California the following weekend.

There was just one problem. Their friend subsequently suffered a knee injury and withdrew from the experiment. But Mary and Andrew had already committed. Their flights and accommodation were booked and the race entries paid for.

“We thought, well, we might as well go,” Mitchell recalls. “How bad can it be?”

They also had the encouragement – or perhaps bad influence – of American friends Jill and Dougin Walker, serial Ironman competitors who have completed around 100 Ironmans apiece.

“We’ve fallen in with a bad crowd,” she jokes.

For Mitchell, who has completed around 30 Ironmans since her first in 2004, racing twice in eight days was uncharted territory. The closest she had previously come was roughly a month between Kona and Ironman Malaysia.

But Mitchell also had another reason to make the most of Kona.

Mitchell had previously won her age group at the Ironman World Championship in 2019. Since then, however, her attempts to return to the top of the podium had been repeatedly derailed.

In 2022, she was hit by a car while riding on the Queen Ka’ahumanu Highway just 10 days prior, preventing her from starting the race.

In 2024, at the women’s World Championship in Nice, she developed food poisoning the night before the race and abandoned roughly 140 kilometers into the bike.

Then in 2025, she returned to Kona, only to discover that what she initially believed to be a cold was COVID. She struggled throughout the race and eventually withdrew on the run.

“I had three years of thwarted attempts to do the World Championship,” she says.

Heading into 2026, Mitchell and her husband had decided this would be their final Kona appearance. They wanted to experience other races and destinations rather than continue returning to the Big Island.

And for much of the race day, Mitchell’s final Kona appearance looked unlikely to deliver another world title.

Mitchell had hoped to swim around 90 minutes, but the ocean conditions and what she admits was insufficient swim preparation conspired against her. She eventually emerged from Kailua Bay in 1:57:06.

“I had an appalling swim,” she says. “I hadn’t done enough long swimming, didn’t have enough endurance, just because swimming’s not my favorite thing.”

By the time she reached transition, Mitchell had effectively written off her chances of winning: “When I stood up out of the water, I thought, a competitive race is off the table now.”

Rather than chase positions, she decided to enjoy what she believed would be her last Ironman World Championship. Her mantra became simple: “Look after yourself and just keep chipping away at it.”

Despite the heat, wind, and particularly oppressive humidity, Mitchell began making steady progress through the field. She completed the bike in 6:38:10 and started the marathon feeling surprisingly good. She settled into a sustainable pace, making sure to take in adequate fluids and calories at every aid station.

With her husband, Andrew, also competing, there was nobody on the sidelines feeding her information about her position. It wasn’t until she reached the top of the Energy Lab, with roughly 12 kilometers remaining, that an acquaintance delivered some unexpected news.

“She said, ‘You’re first and running faster than anyone else in your age group.’ And I’m like, ‘What? No, come on.’”

Mitchell completed the marathon in 4:23:23, the fastest run in her age group, to secure her second age-group world title.

Ordinarily, the next few days would have been devoted to celebrating, recovering and enjoying the satisfaction of a long-awaited victory. Instead, she had another Ironman looming.

Following the Kona awards dinner and a celebratory glass of wine, Mary and Andrew flew to Sacramento, arriving on Monday with less than a week remaining before their next race.

There was no elaborate recovery protocol, no special preparation, and definitely no attempt to squeeze in additional fitness.

“We rode our bikes for an hour to an hour and a half along the river trail a couple of times, which was really nice,” Mitchell recalls.

The rides were deliberately easy, simply turning their legs over while enjoying the scenery and wildlife. She also completed a couple of short runs no longer than 30 minutes or demanding.

Her only swim was a brief dip in the river to test the water temperature and a new wetsuit, purchased after her previous one split during a 70.3 race in Leipzig, Germany, earlier in the trip.

More surprisingly, Mitchell wasn’t experiencing any crippling muscle soreness she remembered from her earlier Ironman days.

“It’s strange. They sort of ached, but they didn’t actually feel sore,” she explains.

She believes advances in running shoe technology have made a meaningful difference to how her legs feel after an Ironman. She raced in “super shoes” but suspects recovering from back-to-back marathons would have been considerably harder in the shoes available a decade ago.

Still, there was plenty of uncertainty. When asked whether she questioned the wisdom of attempting another Ironman, Mary laughs: “Oh, I thought about that just about every day.”

“If they’d had a half [Ironman] race, I probably would have dropped down to that distance.”

She reasoned that California’s current-assisted, wetsuit-legal swim would be far less demanding than Kona’s ocean swim. The flat, relatively straightforward bike course also appeared manageable.

But the marathon was another matter entirely.

“My big concern throughout the whole week was the run. Can you do two marathons in eight days with having raced in Kona with the conditions that are notoriously one of the more difficult races that you can do?”

Mitchell had trained specifically for Kona and made no adjustments to prepare for the double. Whatever happened in Sacramento would simply happen.

As expected, the California swim was a very different experience. Thanks to the river current and wetsuit, Mitchell emerged from the water in approximately 55 minutes, effectively halving her swim time from Kona.

But the bike wasn’t entirely without incident. Early in the ride, Mitchell developed significant pain in her quadriceps muscle and her shin. By the end of the first 90-kilometer lap, she was seriously considering pulling out.

“I was thinking, should I stop? It’s really quite sore,” she recalls. “Am I causing damage?”

She decided to continue to the next aid station and reassess, knowing she could stop at any point. Eventually, the pain subsided.

With no expectations, and already holding her Kona qualification for the following year, Mitchell approached the rest of the race with an unusually relaxed attitude. She chatted with volunteers, stopped when necessary, and enjoyed the atmosphere.

“I was just chilled the entire race because I didn’t have anything to prove,” she explains.

The marathon, her greatest concern, proved surprisingly manageable. Rather than experiencing the crushing fatigue she had anticipated, Mitchell found herself settling into a rhythm. The crowds were enthusiastic, the aid stations welcoming, and she passed the kilometers chatting with other competitors.

Her marathon time, 4:23:30, was almost identical to the one she had run in Kona eight days earlier. When she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, she had not only completed the experiment but had also won her age group again. Andrew had done the same.

“To our astonishment, we both won our age groups,” Mitchell says.

Perhaps even more surprising was how they felt afterward.

“When we first started this sport, you do an Ironman and basically couldn’t walk for three days. Getting up out of a chair was really difficult and painful.”

This time, within 24 to 48 hours, both felt remarkably normal.

Mitchell discovered triathlon in her 30s, partly because Andrew was already involved in sport and she was tired of being left at home while he trained. She bought a cheap bike, started entering local short-course events and quickly fell in love with the sport and its community.

Her first Ironman came in 2004 at Busselton in Western Australia. Like many newcomers, she initially assumed it would be a one-off experience. More than two decades later, she’s still going.

Now retired and living in Adelaide, Mitchell trains up to 20-25 hours per week during her biggest blocks. She has worked with a coach for many years and increasingly recognizes the importance of strength training and nutrition, particularly in preserving muscle mass as she ages. Around five years ago, she also began working with a sports dietitian to improve her fueling, gut training, and overall nutritional approach.

But Mitchell is quick to point out that endurance sport doesn’t consume her entire existence. She enjoys good food, wine, socializing, reading and traveling with Andrew. And while she is competitive, she says curiosity is an even greater motivation.

“I just want to see how far I can push myself,” she explains.

Since retiring, Mitchell has challenged herself to do “at least one thing each year that takes me out of my comfort zone.”

Last year, that meant racing Patagonman in Chile, confronting her dislike of cold water by jumping from a ferry into a freezing cold fjord to start the race. This year, it was the Kona-California double. Next year, she’s already entered the 100-kilometer Tarawera ultramarathon in New Zealand.

For Mitchell, the biggest reward of the double wasn’t another age-group victory. It was discovering that, at age 67, she could still surprise herself.

“I think it resets your mind. It resets your thinking about what your body can achieve. And what mentally you can achieve,” she reflects.

The experience also reinforced what she loves about triathlon: the places it takes her, the friendships it creates, and the opportunities to challenge assumptions about her own limitations.

“It’s taught me that you’re stronger than you think you are, mentally and physically.”

Would she ever attempt two Ironmans in eight days again?

“No. Absolutely not. There’s no need to repeat the experiment!”

For all the satisfaction of the achievement, Mitchell admits she would have liked more time to savor her second Kona world title. Instead, almost immediately, she was packing up and preparing to race again.

“It would have been nice to just chill and enjoy it a little bit more,” she explains. “Have a couple more glasses of wine, soak it in.”

But the experience did change one thing: Despite initially declaring that 2026 would be their last Kona, Mary and Andrew have both accepted qualifying slots to next year’s World Championship.

#8773. Is Cycling Good Cardio? Here's How It Compares to Running and Swimming

Learn how cycling compares to other cardio activities like walking, running, and swimming.

Riding a bike is as good a workout as it is a ton of fun. Hop on a bike—any kind—and your heart rate will pick up, your breathing rate will increase, and you’ll break a sweat. Whether you choose to fly over asphalt on a road bike, cruise back roads on a gravel setup, or push pedals in an indoor studio, you’re doing your mind and body big favors when you hop in the saddle.

One of the biggest payoffs? Cardio benefits. Read on for how cycling boosts your cardio fitness and how it stacks up to other forms of cardiovascular exercise, like running and using an elliptical.

Cardio exercise is any exercise that increases your heart rate and respiration (breathing rate). Cardio exercise can be aerobic or anaerobic. Broadly, what makes cardio aerobic or anaerobic is the intensity level of the exercise (and physiologically, the source of energy for that exercise).

Aerobic exercise, defined by the American College of Sports Medicine, is a rhythmic activity that uses large muscle groups and can be maintained continuously. This is also called steady-state exercise, and it can include running, walking, cycling, rowing, using the elliptical or stair-stepper, swimming, and hiking.

Anaerobic cardio exercise is high-intensity, and true anaerobic activity can only be performed for short periods of time; sprinting is a good example of anaerobic cardio exercise. Activities like jumping rope and mountain biking—and any of the aforementioned activities performed in high-intensity spurts—can also fit into this cardio category.

In any case, “cardio exercise often consists of extended periods of time with an elevated heart rate and an increase in oxygen demand,” says Alexander Rothstein, ACSM-certified exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning coach, and coordinator for the exercise science program at New York Institute of Technology.

“Performing cardio exercise will stress the cardiovascular system, which will signal the need for adaptation and cause improvements in the body’s ability to supply and utilize oxygen,” he explains.

The goal of cardio exercise is to increase the efficiency of your heart, lungs, and circulatory system, thereby improving your overall fitness and endurance.

“Cardiorespiratory fitness reflects the ability of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to supply oxygen-rich blood to skeletal muscles during sustained physical activity,” says Joe Scarrella, triathlon coach and certified personal trainer at Life Time Chanhassen in Minnesota.

This type of fitness “is vitally important to health and wellness, especially to the ability of engaging in normal activities of daily living without excessive fatigue,” he says. “Because of its heart-strengthening and overall health benefits, cardio training should always be near the top of priorities when allocating time to a fitness program.”

Yes, cycling is cardio exercise—an excellent form of it, in fact. Cycling requires continuous movement that increases your heart rate. When you pedal, your heart works harder to pump blood to your muscles. This steady effort challenges your cardiovascular system, helping it become more efficient over time.

A cycling habit brings about a lot of benefits, including:

While cycling is a fantastic form of cardio, it’s not your only option. Here’s a look at how it measures up to other popular forms of cardio exercise.

Cycling burns more calories per hour than walking, according to the Compendium of Physical Activity. Cycling at a leisurely pace (less than 10 mph) can burn about 330 calories per hour for a 180-pound person. Walking at a leisurely pace (2.5 mph) burns about 246 calories per hour for a person of the same weight.

Both cycling and walking are low-impact exercises, making them ideal for those with joint pain or arthritis. Cycling allows more room for increasing speed or resistance without changing joint impact, which offers a more intense cardio workout for individuals with joint concerns.

On the flip side, walking is a weight-bearing form of exercise, while cycling is not, so walking could be the better choice for individuals with bone density concerns.

Walking is more accessible because it requires no equipment beyond a good pair of shoes. Cycling, on the other hand, requires much more gear: a bike and helmet, at minimum, plus safe space to ride outdoors. An indoor stationary bike or bike trainer is required for cycling inside, and while there are budget options, it’s still an investment.

If you're looking for a simple, accessible form of low-intensity cardio, walking might be the best option. However, for a more intense workout that’s still easy on the joints, cycling is the way to go.

Running tends to burn more calories than cycling, because it’s more difficult for many individuals to achieve the increase in heart rate that they may get from running, Rothstein says. It may take longer to burn as many calories as one would while running.

According to data from the Compendium of Physical Activity, cycling at a “self-selected moderate pace” burns about 573 calories in one hour for a 180-pound person. That same person may burn about 615 calories “jogging at a self-selected pace,” according to the Compendium.

Running is a high-impact exercise, which can place stress on your joints, especially your knees and ankles. Cycling, in contrast, is low-impact, making it a better option for people with joint issues or those recovering from injuries.

Both running and cycling primarily work your lower body, including your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. During cycling, your core and back muscles may be recruited more to maintain posture on the bike, depending on the style of your bike. When running, your core, back, and arms all work to maintain posture and stability.

If joint health is a concern or you prefer a lower-impact workout, cycling is the better choice. Running is a viable option for people who can handle the joint impact and/or don’t have the means to invest in a bike or stationary bike.

Swimming and cycling burn similar amounts of calories, depending on intensity. According to the Compendium of Physical Activity, swimming freestyle at a vigorous pace for one hour burns about 800 calories for a 180-pound person. The same person would burn about 818 calories cycling at 14 to 16 mph, which may be a moderate or vigorous effort depending on your fitness level.

Swimming has virtually no impact on joints because the water supports your body, making it an ideal option for those with joint pain, injuries, or mobility issues.

Cycling is also low-impact but not quite as easy on the body as swimming. Depending on the type of bike, some individuals may struggle with mobility when cycling. (For example, on a road bike with drop bars, it can strain the neck and back to reach them. In such a case, a bike with an upright frame might be a better choice.)

Swimming is a full-body workout, engaging both your upper and lower body, as well as your core. You’ll recruit more muscles in the arms and shoulders while swimming, compared to cycling, which primarily targets the lower body.

If you want a no-impact, full-body workout, swimming might be your best option. Keep in mind that sticking to a swimming plan requires having access to a lap pool, which isn’t feasible for everyone. Even though a bike can be a big investment, it may be the more accessible option in this case.

Cycling burns more calories than elliptical training at the same effort level. For a 180-pound person, cycling at a moderate pace (12 to 14 mph) burns around 654 calories in 60 minutes, while a moderate 60-minute session on the elliptical burns about 409 calories.

Both are low-impact exercises, making them suitable for people with joint concerns. The elliptical may provide an advantage for people who struggle with mobility, because you remain in an upright position and don’t have to significantly flex the spine like on the bike.

Elliptical machines engage both the upper and lower body, while cycling primarily focuses on your lower body, though the upper body and core are still engaged to some extent while riding a bike.

If you prefer a workout that engages your whole body, the elliptical may be the better choice. However, if you like the idea of getting outside and/or exercising with a community, cycling offers a more dynamic experience in that sense.

Overall, “all forms of cardio are similar in their cardiovascular health and weight loss benefits,” says Rothstein. “The increased oxygen demand and overall cardiovascular stress will result in improved health and well-being. The ability to burn calories is also similar even if the rate might be different between types of cardio.”

Adaptations in stamina are where the most significant differences lie, says Rothstein. “We adapt based on the specific training stimulus, so in cyclists, stamina improvements will mostly be shown in cycling performance. For example, if you train cycling, you will not improve your running unless you also train as a runner. This is because even though both have cardiovascular adaptation benefits, the muscular adaptations will be specific to the type of training.”

In other words: Train what you want to be good at doing.
