Earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales. Target 60,000 miles for a one-way business class ticket.

Use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska. Search 331 days out from your desired travel date. Look for flights showing "Partner Award" availability on JAL's calendar.

Verify your target flight operates a Boeing 787 or 777 with JAL's "Sky Suite" business class product. Older aircraft on some routes may have a less desirable cabin configuration. Check SeatGuru or JAL's fleet page.

Phone Alaska's award desk at 1-800-252-7522. Have your dates, route, and JAL flight number ready. The agent will search their system and process the redemption. Expect $25-$50 in taxes and fees.

Log into JAL.com with your confirmation number to select your specific seat and pre-order your meal. JAL offers both Western and Japanese cuisine options in business class, and the Japanese multi-course kaiseki meal is the experience worth choosing.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy Is Your On-Ramp

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

The more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Plan never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

You need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:

Tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

If your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan in the spring — cherry blossom season, the dream itinerary for so many in the ChooseFI community.

The Route: Seattle (SEA) → Tokyo Narita (NRT) on JAL Flight 009, operated by a Boeing 787-9.

The Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

The Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

JAL's inflight service is consistently ranked among the best in the world. The meal service features both Western and Japanese options, sake and premium spirits, and attentive crew who seem genuinely delighted to serve you. The 9–10 hour flight to Narita passes in quiet, restful comfort. You arrive refreshed.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days before departure. For cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and Golden Week (late April through early May), JAL Business Class award space is competitive. Set a calendar reminder and search on JAL.com starting at day 335 — then call Alaska the moment the window opens if you see available seats.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — one of the most underused benefits in the program. On a US-to-Japan routing, you could stop in Tokyo for four or five days, then continue to Osaka or another Japanese city (on a separate ticket), effectively getting a multi-city Japan trip from a single 60,000-mile award. Discuss this with the Alaska agent when booking.

Given Alaska's limited transfer partners, the most reliable path to a large Alaska miles balance is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card, which regularly offers welcome bonuses of 40,000–75,000 miles. Stack two cardholders in your household — you and your partner each earn a welcome bonus — and you have a round-trip business class redemption funded almost entirely from sign-up offers.

Marriott-to-Alaska transfers take 1 to 5 days and are irreversible. Never initiate the transfer until you've confirmed the award space exists on JAL.com. Transferring speculatively and then discovering the seat is gone is a painful and costly mistake.

While JAL does release excellent inventory — hence the availability score of 4 out of 5 — "year round" availability doesn't mean unlimited. Japanese holidays (Golden Week, Obon in August, New Year's) see compressed availability. The best open inventory is typically September through November and January through mid-February.

Alaska's policy is no fuel surcharges on partner awards, but always verify the final tax-and-fee total before giving your credit card number. Your total out-of-pocket should be well under $200 per ticket. If it's higher, ask the agent to itemize.

This redemption is built for the ChooseFI couple or solo traveler who has been intentionally accumulating Alaska miles — or Marriott Bonvoy points — and wants to experience transpacific Business Class without the $8,000 price tag. If Japan is on your bucket list and you're willing to do a phone call to complete the booking, this is one of the highest-value redemptions in the entire loyalty ecosystem.

Minimum points needed: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. A couple needs 120,000 miles for two one-way Business Class tickets.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — and that rating is honest. It's not beginner-friendly (rated 2 out of 5 for beginners), but it's absolutely achievable for anyone willing to learn the two-step process. **What makes it moderate:** First, earning Alaska miles is less straightforward than earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex points. Alaska has **no direct credit card transfer partners** in the major bank ecosystems, which means you can't funnel everyday Amex or Chase spend into Alaska miles directly. You're relying on Alaska co-branded credit cards or the Marriott Bonvoy transfer path. Second, partner award bookings **cannot be completed online** — you must call Alaska Mileage Plan. For travelers accustomed to booking everything digitally, this feels like friction. In practice, the call takes 15–20 minutes with a prepared agent and is genuinely straightforward. Third, while availability is rated 4 out of 5 (excellent by transpacific standards), you still need to plan ahead, particularly for peak Japan travel seasons. **Three tips to make it easier:** 1. **Start with the Alaska Airlines Visa card** — it's the most direct route to a large Alaska miles balance and regularly offers competitive welcome bonuses. 2. **Do your availability research on JAL.com before calling** — walk into that phone call with the flight number, date, and cabin class already confirmed. The booking becomes a five-minute transaction. 3. **Book 6–10 months out** for peak dates — this eliminates most of the availability stress and gives you time to transfer points if needed. If you've already booked one partner award by phone with any airline, this will feel familiar. If this is your first, the effort is absolutely worth it for a redemption worth 8–17 cents per point.

No. Alaska Mileage Plan is not a transfer partner of Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards. Your primary earning paths are the Alaska Airlines credit card, Marriott Bonvoy transfers, and purchasing miles during Alaska's periodic sales.

No. JAL flights booked with Alaska miles do not carry fuel surcharges. You will pay only government taxes and fees, typically $25-$50 for a one-way transpacific ticket. This is a major advantage over booking through some other programs.

The best availability appears right at the 331-day booking window. Shoulder seasons like January-February and September-November tend to have more open seats. Cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and summer are the most competitive periods.

Marriott Bonvoy points transfer to Alaska at a 3:1 ratio. For every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred, you receive 20,000 Alaska miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus, totaling 25,000 Alaska miles. To reach 60,000 Alaska miles, you would need approximately 135,000 Bonvoy points (factoring in the bonus on each 60K tranche).

Alaska Mileage Plan to JAL business class is one of the best-kept sweet spots in travel rewards. At 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges, you get access to a world-class cabin at roughly half the mileage cost of competing programs. The earning path is narrower than programs with multiple transfer partners, but for anyone willing to build Alaska miles intentionally, the 8-13 cents per mile value on JAL business class to Japan is extraordinarily difficult to beat.

#8770. Choosing a Gravel Bike? These 12 Editor-Tested Models Deliver the Tire Clearance, Geometry, and Value That Matter

From bikepacking to gravel racing, these tested bikes cover every kind of dirt-road ride.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Instead of riding busy, congested city and suburban roads, many cyclists now head to lightly traveled gravel and unimproved roads. Gravel riding is a great way to see beautiful fall foliage, enjoy the fresh air, and avoid traffic. Most brands sell at least one gravel model; some offer multiple gravel platforms or bikes designed for particular gravel-riding niches. Whether you need a new bicycle for a big gravel fondo or race, a versatile bike for multi-surface rides, or a rig for bikepacking adventures, there’s a gravel bike for you.

The term “gravel riding” is very broad and doesn’t necessarily mean riding on gravel surfaces the entire ride. Gravel rides can include anything from hard-packed dirt roads (which you can often ride on a traditional road bike) to singletrack trails (typically associated with mountain bikes). Gravel riding also includes almost any other type of unimproved roadway; forest access roads, farm roads, jeep roads, rail trails, and canal paths are all commonly lumped under the gravel umbrella. And many of the best gravel routes and events incorporate a few of these surfaces.

Because they get ridden in such varied terrain, gravel bikes come in many shapes and sizes. They span the gamut of aero-optimized bikes that look similar to WorldTour road bikes to full suspension models that resemble mountain bikes with dropbars—But most gravel bikes fall somewhere in between these polar extremes. Most gravel bikes share a few key traits: Generous tire clearance, a more upright riding position, and geometry that prioritizes stability and confidence on rough surfaces.

Buying Tip: Don’t pass on a great gravel bike because you don’t like its tires. Focus on a bike’s tire clearance rather than the stock rubber’s tread or width. Brands usually equip gravel bikes with tires that work well in average conditions. If those tires don’t work for you, it’s a simple fix. Upgrading to tires that better suit your needs is often the best—and easiest—first change you can make, and it usually shaves weight.

The Canyon Grizl is a great all-arounder. It’s a gravel bike built for all sorts of adventures, whether it’s a casual after-work gravel spin, commuting around town, or a multi-day bikepacking trip. The SRAM Apex XPLR 1x12 drivetrain shifts quickly and has a wide gear range. The Grizl’s carbon frame also helps dampen the bumps on rougher roads and trails.

Since we tested the bike a few seasons ago, platform updates have improved its capability and appeal. The Grizl now features clearance for wider tires (up to 56mm), internal downtube storage, and an easily sourced UDH hanger. If this model doesn't speak to you, Canyon offers several Grizl options priced from $1,899 to $4,699.

If you don’t have thousands of dollars to spend but need a bike for riding actual gravel roads, your choices might seem limited. However, if you dig into brands’ websites and look for budget picks, you will find a few gems. The $1,300 Salsa Journeyer Essa is a good example; it stands out for its robust parts, wide tires, and size range.

Unlike some cheaper gravel bikes you may find on Amazon, the Journeyer’s aluminum frame comes in six sizes to fit riders from 4’8” to 6’5”. Additionally, it’s available through REI. This way, you’ll have warranty support if anything goes awry, and the bike is professionally assembled (if you choose in-store pickup).

For components, Salsa equips this Journeyer model with Shimano’s 1x8-speed Essa group (including Shimano mechanical disc brakes)—the parts aren’t fancy, but they’re robust. The only negative point of the Journeyer Essa is its standard QR dropouts, which make upgrading to lighter-weight or tubeless wheels slightly more difficult.

The Topstone 1 is Cannondale’s top-tier aluminum gravel bike. Designed for versatility and adventure, it’s equally at home on pavement or dirt, with a utilitarian setup that includes mounts for racks, bags, fenders, and extra bottles—perfect for long-haul rides. But don’t mistake utilitarian for boring; the Topstone still feels lively and efficient on the road, making it a great choice for days when your rides lean more toward pavement.

This model comes with 37mm tires, but the frame clears up to 45mm rubber. This allows you to choose tires for the terrain and rides you take. The Shimano GRX 2x11 drivetrain is another standout, offering a wide gear range for steep, rough climbs while keeping gear jumps tight—something you’ll appreciate when riding extended stretches of pavement.

Salsa practically invented the modern gravel bike with its Warbird, and the Minnesota-based brand remains as relevant as ever. Its recently launched Flyway C is a lightweight and responsive gravel bike for gravel racing or all-day rides. It features generous tire clearance (up to 57mm), a UDH dropout (for easy replacement or upgrades), and revised geometry (long reach and short stem) for improved control on rough terrain.

Several Flyway configurations are available (I tested the Force AXS XPLR model), and I think the Apex Eagle AXS model sits right in the sweet spot for many riders. As the name suggests, Salsa outfits this bike with a combination of SRAM’s Apex AXS and Eagle X1 AXS 1x electronic drivetrains to provide a superwide gear range. In addition to the great components, Salsa also equips this model with a flared carbon bar and a carbon seatpost. It’s an all-around great package for anyone looking to up their gravel game this season.

Trek’s Checkpoint ALR 5 is versatile, well-rounded, and a great pick for riders new to gravel cycling. In his review, Chabanov says, “The value sweet spot: modern geometry and feature set borrowed from the [Checkpoint] SL, delivered in a durable alloy package with smart mounts and standards—at a starting price that leaves room in the budget for meaningful upgrades. Because there are no proprietary parts, upgrading and swapping things like the handlebar, stem, and seatpost is super easy.”

Overall, the Checkpoint ALR gets far more right than it gets wrong. Sure, you can nitpick the stock wheels and tires—or wish for the carbon model’s downtube storage and IsoSpeed—but those trade-offs help keep the price in check while preserving what matters. This bike has confident handling, generous tire room, real-world durability, and an upgrade-friendly platform. The result is a thoroughly well-thought-out aluminum gravel bike that feels ready for anything from weeknight dirt spins to loaded weekend overnighters, or even that gravel race that’s on your bucket list.

If you’re a gravel racer on a budget, or simply like going fast and don’t have the money for bikes like the Specialized S-Works Crux or Colnago G5-X, Canyon’s new Grail should be on your short list. As my colleague Matt Phillips described in his review of the revised platform, “And “fast” was the word that stuck with me as I rode the Grail across singletrack, dirt roads, and paved roads. It feels fast. It made me feel like I was fast.”

Wide tire clearance is one of the latest Grail’s upgrade highlights. At 57mm, the frame and fork can fit the widest gravel tires and even 29 x 2.25-inch mountain bike rubber for rocky terrain or singletrack (or if you want a super comfortable feel). The entry-tier Grail CF SL models use a heavier carbon frame than the Grail CFR and CF SLX versions, but only 140 grams more than the high-end CFR bike (about the weight of a standard butyl inner tube). All models feature a carbon cockpit, seatpost, and wheels.

The Grail CF 7 Speed is a great bang-for-the-buck gravel racer. Canyon equips it with SRAM’s excellent Rival XPLR AXS 1x13 electronic shifting gravel groupset. Although Canyon doesn’t ship this model with a power meter, you can easily upgrade to a Rival power crank for under $200.

You’re not buying this bike for its tire clearance, gear-hauling options, or aerodynamics; plenty of other gravel bikes do those things better than the G5-X. You buy this bike because it’s a Colnago.

On fast gravel roads, double track, and even technical singletrack, Colnago’s superb geometry, fit, and ride comfort won me over. The G5-X feels super composed and planted when descending and over choppy gravel road sections. The bike is precise and refined—pick your line and take it. On climbs and rolling terrain, the G5-X is comfortable and efficient, and responds immediately to bursts of power.

Overall, Colnago’s latest bike is a beautifully fast gravel racer with sublime handling. However, while the G5-X has more tire clearance (53mm) than the brand’s previous gravel offerings, it falls a few millimeters shy of the clearance found on some new gravel models. This will matter to some, but many riders will seek out the G5-X for the name on the downtube and Colnago’s cycling legacy.

Inspired by the Tour Divide—America’s longest mountain bike race—this bike carries more and handles a wider range of terrain than almost any other gravel bike. It’s loaded with mounts for racks, camping gear, bike accessories, and water bottles.

Although it’s intended for burly rides, the Cutthroat features a carbon frame and fork, which helps to reduce weight. And Salsa’s Class 5 Vibration Reduction System absorbs uneven terrain for a more comfortable ride. The Cutthroat C GRX model also includes a Shimano GRX 1x12 mechanical, wide-range drivetrain and a dropper seatpost.

With its steel frame, bar-end shifters, and triple-chainring crankset, the Masi Giramondo is a throwback to a bygone era of bicycle design and construction. While the bike’s aesthetic and features might not appeal to athletes chasing fast finishing times in 200-mile gravel races, it’s perfect for riders who want to hit the gravel, dirt, or paved roads loaded down with gear for touring adventures.

Unlike most bikes sold for touring or bikepacking, the Giramondo comes stock with a front and rear rack. This means you won’t have to add them to your bike-buying budget. To make it slightly easier to pedal your fully laden bike up hills, Masi equips this model with a triple crankset. While triples aren’t as trendy as 1x drivetrains, they offer an extremely wide gear range: Its lowest gear is close to many mountain bikes, and the highest gear rivals many gravel race bikes.

While State labels this model “All-Road,” it’s very much a modern gravel bike. Starting at $2,400 for a complete bike, or $1,400 for the frameset, the All-Road Carbon checks all of the boxes without totally draining your bank account. It accommodates up to 2.2-inch tires (complete builds ship with 50mm Vittoria T50s), is UDH-compatible, and takes a T47 bottom bracket. The All-Road Carbon also features internal storage in the frame’s downtube with a Fidlock magnetic latch.

The Carbon All-Road’s frame isn’t super aero-shaped, and it doesn’t use funky proprietary parts—and that’s a good thing. This bike is made for riders who prioritize durability and functionality over flashy graphics, pro teams, and marketing hype. The All-Road’s geometry falls on the “race-inspired” end of the spectrum, compared with the more upright feel of adventure-style gravel bikes. The bike carries speed on hardpack dirt and gravel and feels adequately stiff when sprinting and out of corners. The ride quality is a little harsher than premium gravel offerings, but a complete Carbon All-Road costs less than most big-name brands’ frames.

The all-new Specialized Crux has shed its cyclocross roots and turned into a modern gravel racer. In his review of the fifth-generation platform, Test Editor Dan Chabanov says, “It is built around the demands of professional gravel racers, and around the idea that going fast off-road now means balancing low weight, aero efficiency, tire clearance, and stability rather than just chasing the lightest possible frame.” The result is an excellent gravel bike that, while optimized for racers, anyone who loves going fast can enjoy.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips rode the Crux 5 for several days on the gravel roads in Durango, Colorado, and walked away very impressed by the updated bike. “The Crux 5 leans more toward stability and predictability,” he said. “It’s fast, yes. Very fast. But it’s also composed. It lets you settle in. It doesn’t feel like it’s trying to prove something every second.”

That balance is a big part of what makes the Crux great for non-racers. “A lot of us don’t need a gravel bike that only makes sense at 300 watts,” Phillips said. “We need a bike that feels sharp when you want to go hard, but isn’t a pain in the ass the rest of the time.”

Of the five models in the Crux 5 lineup, the Crux 5 Comp stands out for its performance-to-price ratio. It features a slightly heavier carbon frame than the high-end S-Works variants, but it has the same great geometry, tire clearance, and aerodynamics. Specialized equips the Comp model with SRAM’s excellent Rival AXS XPLR 1x brakes and drivetrain, and the bike rolls on 26mm-wide inner diameter alloy wheels wrapped in 45mm-wide Pathfinder tubeless tires.

The bike used by two-time gravel World Champion Marianne Vos (🐐), the Áspero-5 is what happens when Cervélo combines aerodynamic principles of the Paris-Roubaix-winning S5 with a gravel race bike. This bike is eye-wateringly fast on smoother gravel and dirt roads. The Áspero-5 is fast enough that many riders will want to use it on paved roads too.

Much of this speed advantage comes from Cervélo’s aerodynamic tuning of the frame, fork, and bar; the 42mm-wide Vittoria Corsa Pro Control TLR rubber enhances it. An excellent road tire for broken pavement in narrow sizes, the Pro Control really shines in the 700x42c size on dirt and gravel surfaces.

With so many types and sub-niches of gravel bikes, it can seem overwhelming to pick the right one. My first advice: start by honestly evaluating the terrain you ride, then consider how you like to ride it. From there, narrow your choices to the bikes that meet your budget, personal tastes, and other factors.

Racing-oriented bikes typically feature an aggressive fit and handling with fewer mounts for bags or extra water bottles. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes built for long-distance, multi-day adventures, equipped with all the mounts you could want for gear and accessories. In between, there’s a wide range of subtle variations that can make a big difference.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8769. Locust Pose Might Be a Simple Backbend, But It Can Help Improve Your Posture

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about the backbend Locust Pose first appeared in the July-August 1996 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

If a picture is worth a thousand words, then our posture speaks volumes. Poor carriage of the torso—rounded shoulders, sunken chest, and a downward cast of the eyes—generally suggests a negative state of being. Good posture, on the other hand—shoulders rolled back and down, chest lifted, and an energetic carriage—demonstrates confidence and a sense of purpose.

All the backbending yoga postures help create this physical expression of assurance. You feel better, have more energy, and benefit from an enhanced respiratory system. The internal alignment of the organs is refined as we adjust and improve the external alignment.

The postures actually have the potential to positively and profoundly affect you on all levels: physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual. Approaching your asanas with this awareness is the key to the enrichment of your practice.

The repertoire of backbending postures, or hyperextensions of the spine, is vast. In this article, we are going to focus on one of the more basic back-bending poses, Grasshopper or Locust Pose (Salabhasana). There are several variations of this posture, according to different systems or styles of hatha yoga. We will practice two versions of Locust, beginning with Salabhasana One as described in B.K.S. Iyengar’s Light on Yoga.

Locust is excellent for correcting poor posture, as well as for counteracting the development of kyphosis, the rounding of the upper back. It tones the whole posterior of the body, strengthens the abdominals, and enhances digestion.

Begin by lying face down on your mat, with your arms at your sides near your hips, palms facing upward. Tuck your chin in, forehead on the floor.

Engage your abdominals by drawing your navel in and up, to stabilize your lower back. Contract your buttocks and quadriceps. Keep the knees, legs, and feet together. Exhale the breath as you simultaneously raise the head, chest, arms, and legs. Look forward and up. Hold and breathe for five to 10 seconds. Keep the abdominals firm so you feel the support from underneath.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position. Turn your head to the side and completely relax. Repeat once or twice more.

Full Locust begins in the same base position, but with the arms outstretched at shoulder level, perpendicular to the body. The palms are facing down, and the chin is on the mat. The knees, legs, and feet are together.

Engage your abdominal muscles by drawing your navel in and up; contract your buttocks and quadriceps. This time, inhale the breath as you raise the arms, chest, head, and legs. Look forward and up. Breathe naturally as you hold the posture for five to 10 seconds. Keep your shoulders away from your earlobes as you continue to stretch your arms back and slightly upward. Palms remain facing the floor. The idea is to lift the entire body upward as you balance on the center of your abdomen.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position, and relax. Repeat once or twice more.

If your lower back is sensitive or you are prone to chronic neck tension, you may want to practice the pose in the following stages.

Lie on your stomach, face down, arms at your sides near your hips. Palms are facing up, the chin is tucked in, and the forehead is on the floor. Legs are hip-distance apart. Firm the buttocks and abdominals as well as the quadriceps.

Inhale the breath. Exhaling, raise just the arms to about hip level, keeping the palms facing up. The head remains on the floor. Lengthen the neck and focus on strengthening your back muscles. Feel your shoulder blades pull down your back and slightly together.

Keep the abdominals, buttocks, and legs firm. Exhale and lower down.

Next, repeat what you’ve just done and add the lifting of the chest. The neck and head will come up as well, but keep looking downward so the neck remains extended rather than arched. Inhale in your base position. Exhale and raise the arms only. Inhale and hold. Ex-haling, raise the chest. Again, hold and breathe rhythmically for five to 10 seconds. Exhale as you lower down.

In the same beginning position, inhale the breath, and exhale raising the arms up. Hold and inhale. Exhale, raising the chest. Hold and inhale. Finally, exhale and raise the legs. Hold and breathe. Keep looking at the floor, focusing on lengthening the body from the top of your head to your fingertips on down to your toes. When you’re ready, lower down on an exhalation. Turn your head to the side, release the pose completely, and relax.

A natural inclination after performing a back bend is to pull your knees to your chest. So after your last repetition, you may want to got into Child’s Pose: Kneel back onto your heels, folding your torso over your thighs with your head resting on the floor in front of your knees. Arms are at your sides with palms facing up.

If your head doesn’t rest on the floor easily, simply fold your arms underneath your forehead for support.

#8767. 5 Signs You’ve Graduated From Beginner Cyclist Status

“When did you first realize you weren’t a beginner anymore?”

It’s a question I posed to my coworkers at Bicycling, many of whom have been riding and racing for multiple decades, at elite levels, across staggering distances, possibly uphill both ways in the snow.

I expected my inbox to be flooded with inspiring anecdotes; tales of triumph and woe; or at the very least, smug hot takes on when it’s OK to start caring about insider stuff like embro and VO2 Max.

But such was not the case. “Oh, I still feel like a beginner almost every day,” was the almost universal, almost completely BS response.

While I admired the humility, based on how many times my colleagues have teased me about my sock height alone, I knew all that self-effacement was completely false. So I pushed back, and eventually they coughed up a few earnest responses.

In many ways, they’re right—it’s great to never lose that wide-eyed rookie sense of discovery and fun. But it’s also pretty cool to see those little glimpses of progress along the way.

If you’re anything like us, here’s how you might have guessed you were starting to get a handle on this whole bicycle-riding thing, no matter how much chain grease might be stamped across your calves.

It’s officially the off-season. In Ohio, we’re having the best fall, where no one complains about the weather (rare for Ohioans) and no wind or rain storms have blown through, robbing us of the vibrant change in the leaves. Hiking is a staple way to enjoy the crunchy leaves, swimming has moved fully indoors, and biking has a sort of leisure to it that it doesn’t have when the landscape is green.

As we slow down and explore other outdoor hobbies in the coming months, here’s a look at the gear our editors are reaching for.

This might seem like an unusual choice for a triathlete, but as the race season winds down and we transition from workouts to just-getting-out, I find myself blasting all of my tempo trainers to the back of my closet in favor of this pair of Jeep-wheel-level all-terrain crushers. For those unfamiliar with Norda, the Canadian brand hit the scene in 2021 (bad timing, sorry) with the release of their ultra-premium — read: ultra-expensive — $285 shoe dubbed the 001. Folks had a field day with the high price, but few could deny that the 001 was something different than what was out there already.

Fast forward to today, and Norda is still (crazy) expensive, but they also still offer shoes that are entirely novel in the increasingly crowded trail running shoe world. The 055 was released earlier this summer as a maximal take on the well-loved, but race-focused 005. For me, I love how you can point your foot at literally anything and the thick-but-stable base will eat it up. Better yet, the woven gaiter adds another layer of stability and protection, meaning you don’t really have to think much about where you put your feet, allowing me to, quite simply, zone out and enjoy the view. And that’s what fall “training” is all about, anyway.

Winter is coming, which in Phoenix means two things: socks come out of storage, and they better be day-glo. Because I live and train downtown, where traffic is abundant and drivers are always (always!) distracted, I dress as obnoxiously as possible to make sure they see me. That means neon fabrics, reflective materials, and LED lights on as many points as possible.

Years ago, I interviewed a safety expert who said you especially want these materials on the parts of your body that move he most when you ride or run, as movement is more likely to catch the eye of a driver. These bright socks have reflective yarn woven into the fabric, making my legs easier to spot on rides and runs. They’re comfortable, they stay up, and they stand up to multiple runs and laundry cycles each week.

Do I look like a 90s fever dream in my neon wardrobe? I sure do. But you’ll see me coming from a mile away, and that’s the whole point.

I haven’t had long hair in the 14 years I’ve been a triathlete — until now. I hate the feeling of hair skimming my neck or swishing back and forth as I run, so it has to be all the way up in the ugliest messy bun. Basically, I’m the opposite of Marjolaine Pierré.

I found that the Goody ComforFlex holds my hair well without pulling, no matter the intensity of workouts. And I don’t end up with tons of hair wrapped around them, which leads me to believe they are keeping my hair at least somewhat healthy despite regular chlorine exposure and frequent washes.

They’ve also held up well, so I can use the same one for at least a month before replacing it.

I’m ashamed to admit I’ve been one of *those* triathletes showing up at the local bike shop, frazzled and looking for the nearest mechanic, then frantically explaining how my seat clamp fell down my downtube and lodged itself somewhere seemingly impossible to reach. Yes, this happened to me at Ironman Chattanooga last year. As someone who prides myself on fixing my own bike issues, this was and still is my worst nightmare.

But I know I’m not alone. Between packing and trying to fit in final workouts ahead of travel, we triathletes can make some poor choices. Add to it that we’re limited in what tools we can bring to fix the problems we create, and it’s a recipe for disaster. Even when we have room and enough weight left to throw them in the bag, we often rush the pack job and toss them in without much organization.

After Chattanooga, I vowed to be more prepared. That’s when a friend showed me this trusty little roll-up tool bag that they use for camping. Small enough that it doesn’t take up all the room, big enough to fit what I need, and cheap enough to buy one for myself and a friend. It was the perfect recommendation.

And the best thing is you don’t have to travel for triathlon to get use out of it. Mine hangs in the garage when I’m home, and I use it every time I work on my bike.

— Travis Mundell, social media strategist

#8762. 7 Knee-Strengthening Exercises That Prevent Pesky Knee Pain

Don’t let a twinge slow down your pedal stroke—or keep you out of the saddle.

Because cycling isn’t a high-impact sport, you’d be forgiven for thinking your knees are safe. But Tara Parsons, a USAC-certified cycling coach and Rapha Women’s Ambassador says she hears riders complaining about knee pain all the time. In fact, 23 percent of riders experience knee pain, according to a study of 116 professional cyclists—and you can bet that number is higher among amateurs.

The knee acts as a hinge between the hip and the ankle, so just think about how many times you flex and extend your knees during a ride. “If you’re missing 5 percent of your range or in a position that’s slightly less than ideal, a small issue can turn into a big problem for someone who's averaging 50,000 reps a weekend,” says Dane DeLozier, the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance in Boulder, CO.

“This, in combination with a lifestyle that involves sitting at desks all day, can cause the weakening of muscles of the trunk, such as the core, glutes, and hips,” adds Parsons.

From there, it’s a domino effect: “When those muscles become weak or underused, they can become inactive or underactive. And when that happens, the muscles that you use a lot on the bike, such as the quads, end up overcompensating. This overcompensation causes poor knee tracking and poor alignment throughout the pedal stroke, which can lead to knee pain,” says Parsons. And that’s not even considering the stress you’re putting on your knees if your bike isn’t fit correctly or if you’re positioning in the saddle is out of whack.

Pay attention to pain in the patellar tendon, the tendon right on the front of the knee, and the IT band, which goes from the hip down to the knee, says DeLozier—those are common areas for pain, irritation, and inflammation that can hamper knee movement. “If that irritation persists, it’s probably best to go see a PT or your physician to figure out what the root cause is,” he adds.

Whether you’re currently dealing with pain or not, it’s important to build up strength around the joint. Strength training off the bike is crucial to developing those muscles. Plus, “your weekly strengthening routine should involve not just strengthening and activation, but also foam rolling or other type of soft tissue manipulation and mobilization” to keep your muscles in peak condition, says Parsons.

Not sure where to start? These knee-strengthening exercises will help you pedal on pain-free.

How to do this knee-strengthening exercise: Perform 2 to 3 sets of each exercise two times per week. You will need a resistance band loop, a Bosu trainer, and a medium weight. An exercise mat is optional.

The exercises in this workout are demonstrated below by Noam Tamir, certified strength and conditioning specialist and founder of TS Fitness in New York City, so you can learn the proper form. Follow along in the video above with Brian Levine, USAT Level 1 coach and endurance athlete.

Place a resistance band loop around legs just above the knee. Lie on your left side with knees bent, and ankles, knees, and hips stacked. Rest your head on left hand to avoid straining your neck and rest right hand on mat in front of you. Keeping your heels together, rotate right knee up toward ceiling as much as possible. Return to starting position. Complete 15 reps, then repeat on right side.

Lie faceup on the mat with a resistance band loop around your legs just above the knees and knees bent, heels close to butt, arms at sides. Contract glutes, and press into heels to lift hips up toward ceiling so your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees as you simultaneously press knees out to keep them in line with hips and maintain tension on the band. Pause. Lower and repeat for 10 to 15 reps.

Start standing on a Bosu trainer with hands on hips for balance. Take a big step back with left foot and lower into a lunge with right leg forming a 90-degree angle. Press through right heel to return left leg to start. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on other leg.

Place a band around ankles and stand with feet hip-width apart so band is taut. Lower into a micro squat, then step out to the left. Bring right foot in so feet are hip-width apart again; continue walking, taking 15 steps to the left before reversing to take 15 steps to the right, keeping the band taut the entire time.

Start standing and holding a kettlebell or medium weight in right hand. Shift weight onto left leg and micro bend left knee. Hinge at the hips as you lower weight to floor and extend right leg back behind you for balance. Continue lowering the weight until you are about parallel to the floor while keeping back straight. Return to the starting position. Repeat for 10 to 15 reps then switch sides.

Start on all fours with wrists under shoulders, knees under hips, toes tucked, and back flat. While keeping knee bent, lift right heel up as if to “stamp” your footprint on the ceiling. Return to starting position. Complete 15 reps then repeat on left side.

Start on all fours with wrists under shoulders, knees under hips, toes tucked, and back flat. Extend right arm and left leg straight out until they’re parallel to the floor. Maintain a flat back, level hips, and focus on pulling your belly button toward your spine. Return to all fours, then raise left arm and right leg. Continue alternating for 90 seconds.

GIFs: Julia Hembree Smith; Video: David Monk, Joshua Wolff

#8759. The Best Bike Lights for Triathletes in 2026, Tested and Reviewed

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Bottom Line: Each of the bike lights in our Best Bike Lights of 2026 list below has been tested on long rides by an experienced triathlete for many miles. Our reviewer is unbiased, with no brand relationships, meaning no brand has paid to appear in our list.

It’s that time of year again. You glance at your training plan, realize your post-work ride slot will now be taking place in the dark, and suddenly “bike light” jumps to the top of your shopping list. The good news is that bike lights in 2026 are significantly better than offerings from just a few years ago. You could even say they are light-years ahead (pun intended) of the bike lights from the 20th century. They are brighter, lighter, and – critically for triathletes – easier to mount on your bike than ever before.

But before you order the cheapest bike light on Amazon, there’s a bit more to think through. The cheapest option is far from the best, but you also don’t need to take out a second mortgage to buy a bike light either. Here’s what actually matters when buying lights as a triathlete, followed by the best options on the market right now.

As a light-toting triathlete, your goal isn’t just to see the road ahead of you; it is also to be seen. Public roads are far from perfectly safe, especially in today’s phone-addicted world filled with distracted drivers. But thankfully, having a bike light is one of the best ways to gain the attention of nearby drivers, reminding them to slow down and give you space as they pass by.

When shopping for a bike light, you want to consider two different design priorities, and pay close attention because most lights optimize for one or the other. First, you want a bike light that shines a powerful beam down the road, illuminating your path at speed in the dark. Second, you want a light that is designed to be seen. These lights use wide-angle optics, lateral emission, and attention-grabbing flash patterns to make you visible to cross-traffic and drivers approaching from the rear. Ideally, your bike light(s) do both.

For triathletes specifically, the lighting challenge runs deeper than a single unit on your bicycle. You might actually want three different lights for the corresponding sports. The ideal setup might include front and rear coverage on the bike, a headlamp or chest light for early-morning runs, and some form of visibility for open-water swims, especially those before sunrise. Each sport requires different hardware, but in this guide, we’ll focus on bike lights. Let’s help you figure out how to sort and sift through the hundreds of options on the market.

The standard brightness unit for sports lights is lumens. The higher the number, the brighter the light. But brighter isn’t always better. Some brands love to advertise max lumens at maximum output, but that can drain the battery in under two hours. Always check the light’s runtime at the mode you’ll actually use.

Consider the type of darkness you’ll be riding in, and how much light you’ll need. Not every triathlete will train in pitch darkness, so here is a quick reference of what you’ll find on the light market:

A pinpoint beam aimed straight ahead is great for one thing, and that’s seeing directly in front of you. But if you’re riding in the dark, you also want to have side visibility, not just from your own perspective, but for other riders and drivers to see you. The best bike lights have a wide spread beam that alerts drivers approaching from angles, not just head-on. Some lights now use multiple LEDs, which is worth considering if you ride in the dark year-round.

This is one of the most important aspects of a bike light because if the battery dies while you are riding in the dark 20 miles from home, you are SOL. Most bike lights are USB-C rechargeable, but runtime varies enormously. If you don’t get a light with a low-battery warning (ideally with several minutes of reserve before shutdown), make sure you keep tabs on how long you’ve been running it before it’s time to recharge.

This is where triathletes diverge from road cyclists. Aero bars, clip-on extensions, and non-standard cockpit shapes make standard clamp mounts useless in many setups. When shopping for lights, you’ll want to look for options that come with flexible silicone straps, GoPro-style mounts, or Garmin quarter-turn compatibility. Silicone straps cover the widest range of setups and are easy to transfer between bikes.

In the 2026 bike light market, there are a number of smart features that come with some of the more pristine options. Some of the features are just bells and whistles, but a few are genuinely helpful, especially for triathletes. Radar integration (Garmin Varia), ANT+ connectivity, automatic brightness adjustment, and brake-sensing technology are popular features that help improve function and safety on the bike. These are not marketing gimmicks – radar in particular can dramatically improve your confidence when riding on open roads with traffic.

Front light placement can be the trickiest part of lighting your tri bike. You can choose between below the basebar (the most aerodynamic option), midway down the aerobars (if the light rotates that direction), and arguably the best solution: adding a computer bridge to your aerobars and mounting the light on top or below it. Whatever you choose, test it on a bumpy road during daylight hours before relying on it in the dark. Remember that you’re not only looking for the light to stay attached, but also for the angle to remain stable as the light illuminates the road in front of you.

Rear lights are much more forgiving, with the seatpost being the most ideal spot for a rear-facing bike light. If you have limited seatpost access, you can mount a light on the seatstay. Just make sure your light is pointing backward rather than toward the sky or floor. If you have bottles or other gear mounted under or behind your seat, make sure they don’t block the bike light when they are fully loaded.

Output: 1,300 lumens front; 90 lumens rear

Battery life: 1.5 hrs front; 4.5 hrs rear

The Ion Pro and Flare bike lights do much more than illuminate through darkness. The paired set uses ANT+ to link the front and rear lights together, and you can control both from a compatible Garmin or Wahoo head unit. Up front, the Ion Pro has up to 1,300 lumens, which is more than enough for most low-light situations. It also has a clean beam pattern with solid front and side visibility, with a few hours of battery life across various power settings. In the rear, the Flare can be used with a 16-degree offset mount option that helps solve one of the most common triathlete problems: mounting a rear light on an angled seatpost or seatstay. The mount is sold separately, but it only costs $5.

Pros: ANT+ integration, offset rear mount solves tri-bike seatpost issues ($5 cost), strong front output Cons: Pricey for a set; front light only has 90 minutes of runtime at max output

Output: 130 to 1,000 lumens with six different modes

Battery life: 120 hrs on ECO FLASH; up to 2 hrs at max output

The Blinder has earned its spot on best-of lists for years, and the 2026 version is no exception. IP67 waterproofing and six different light modes make the Blinder 1000 suitable for a wide range of weather and light conditions, including midnight rain-riding. At low outputs, the Blinder 1000 lasts for days on a single charge. GoPro-style and standard handlebar mounts are both included, making it versatile on almost any tri cockpit.

Pros: Fully IP67 waterproof, versatile mounts, solid build quality, side window visibility

Cons: Heavier than some competitors at the same lumen output

Battery life: 1 hr at max output; up to 60 hrs at minimum output

If your friends call you “Nightrider,” then the AMPP 2200 might be the perfect bike light for you. With a max output of 2,200 lumens, the AMPP 2200 obliterates darkness in a way that can make you feel like you’re riding during the daytime. This is the light for those who ride in pitch darkness at speed, or those who live in extreme daylight climates such as Alaska or Iceland. While its top-end output is impressive, the AMPP 2200 includes different light modes that are ideal for riding in the dusk rather than the pitch black. At 500 to 800 lumens, the AMPP 2200 becomes a practical all-night light with sufficient battery reserve. Its included mount is quite secure, even on rough pavement. The trade-off is weight; at 211g, it’s the heaviest option on this list.

Pros: Exceptional max output, wide runtime range, secure mount, high-quality build

Cons: Heaviest light on this list; 2,200 lumens if overkill for those who don’t ride in complete darkness

Battery life: 4 to 80 hrs (front); 3 to 60 hrs (rear)

If you’re only looking for a pair of lights that will help you be seen, the Knog Frog combo could be the perfect fit. The front light output isn’t enough to illuminate a dark road, but not every triathlete wants to ride in the dark. Sometimes, you just want to be seen by drivers and cross-traffic, especially in low-light conditions. The combo’s battery life is fitting for the price point, and the pair is so light that you won’t even notice them. They come with a flexible silicone strap that wraps around virtually any tube shape, including aero bars. While they won’t light up a country road, the Knog Frog combo is great for being seen in the city, on the bike path, or on a foggy training loop.

Pros: Aero-bar compatible, extremely lightweight, very affordable, easy to use

Cons: 40 lumens won’t illuminate a dark road; not a standalone solution for night riding

Battery life: 16 hrs (day flash mode); 6 hrs (solid mode)

The Varia is a rear light that also functions as a vehicle radar. In terms of safety and security, it is one of the best bike lights on the market. When paired with a compatible Garmin head unit or Varia app, the light alerts you to vehicles approaching from behind, before you can even hear them. It is an incredibly useful safety feature, especially if you frequently ride in groups or on busy roads. If you get nervous riding on open roads, the Varia RTL515 could be the best option for you. While the light function itself isn’t anything special, the radar is the reason to buy it.

Pros: Vehicle radar is a game-changer on open roads; lightweight, impressive battery life, pairs with Garmin ecosystem

Cons: Expensive for a single rear light; radar requires a compatible head unit or phone mount

Battery life: 12 hrs constant; 30 hrs flash

In terms of bang for your buck, it’s hard to beat the Gravity Plus, which uses an accelerometer to detect braking and automatically increases brightness when you decelerate. It is effectively functioning as a brake light, and it is one of the cheapest options on this list. For triathletes who ride out of town, train with unpredictable stop-and-go conditions, or frequent group rides, the brake-sensing rear light is surprisingly effective. Runtime is excellent for a budget light, and you probably won’t even notice the added weight.

Pros: Brake-sensing technology, outstanding battery life, lightweight

Cons: 100 lumens is modest; a brighter light is necessary for riding in complete darkness

#8758. How Yoga Brings You Closer to Yourself and the Life You Want

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about yoga as a science and an art first appeared in the January-February 1977 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Yoga is a science, an art, and a technique which spans the multilevel functioning of the individual. It is a science because of its empirical approach, presented most completely by the classic Yoga Sutras of Patanjali at least 1,000 years ago. Science is defined as a methodology which requires empirical proof of its theories; it requires that which proves a theory be easily repeatable by another experimenter if he/she follows the rules of the experiment.

Yoga, by this definition, is indeed a science. Its rules are given in sutra form and the presentation of Patanjali is a “how-to” book of the highest order. The practitioner need only follow the lead of Patanjali in order to have his own personal empirical results. (It is true that the directions are in parts esoteric and apparently illusive; this points out the necessity of having a teacher upon whom the practioner can rely for advice during certain intervals.) In addition to the work by Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika and the Gheranda and Shiva Samhita are references which can explain the science of yoga.

But yoga is an art, too. Individuals have dedicated their lives to the perfection of this art. This does not necessarily imply the production of tangible output such as texts, although these have been produced in the history of traditional Indian thought. Rather, the use of the word “art” in this context implies the movement toward perfection within, the embodiment of beauty as it can be expressed through the human being. If one dedicates his/her life to the art of yoga, this implies a dedication which does not involve merely daily practice numbering a few hours. Instead, it implies a minute by minute practice which spans years, and some believe, lifetimes of existence.

The art of yoga is the practice of yoga on all levels of existence; this means every thought, action, dream, relationship, food intake, sexual activity, occupation, etc., are brought into the wider perspective of observation in light of the individual’s desire to understand the Self. This understanding does not imply intellectual understanding alone. It implies the “living” or the “being” in the Self rather than just mentally knowing about the Self. One can compare this to the experience of being in a hurricane with merely reading about the experience of a hurricane; the effect would be quite different.

One who lives in the Self has come into a wholeness of being, possibly for us all by virtue of our human existence, but available presently to only a handful due a complex interplay of events which, for whatever reasons, has brought them to a newer threshold of consciousness. Thus the art of yoga lies in bringing perfection into action through becoming one with oneself.

Part of the ability to do this lies with the powerful psychological technique of “acting as if.” If one wishes to meditate, one often begins by acting as if one were meditating. As the form of meditation is assumed, the content of meditation begins to be experienced. If one acts as if one loves another, and acts with sincerity and with honesty, often feelings of love toward that person do begin to flow. So with yoga. If one watches and practices as if yoga were an art and the Self were the artist, then this lends validity to the possibility of this being true.

This brings one to the question of technique. Yoga is also a concrete way of bringing about profound physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual changes within the individual. The student is instructed in yama and niyama (basic ethical precepts), in asanas (meditative postures), in pranayama (conscious voluntary control of the energy associated with breath), in pratyhara and dharana (watching and observing the mind), and finally, in dhyana, or meditation. The final experiencing of samadhi (union) cannot be taught; it is both the result of the foregoing disciplines and independent of them. The understanding of this apparent paradox is part of the process of learning about yoga.

Thus yoga can be seen from the angles of science, art or technique. It can be approached as a small practice of one’s life, or as the way that life is lived, a quality which is brought to live which liberates one from the strong bonds of ego.

#8756. Want to Ride More at Home? These 9 Stationary Bikes Make Training Easy, Quiet, and More Consistent

Find the right at-home ride, whether you want a budget spin bike or a premium smart-bike setup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Weather and daylight don’t always cooperate with our riding schedules. And when we add work hours, family time, yardwork, and life’s daily grind, finding time to ride can feel impossible. Especially during the dark days of late autumn and winter, indoor riding becomes the only realistic option for many of us.

Luckily, indoor cycling is no longer the boring, arduous task it was only a decade ago. Today’s stationary bikes range from no-frills machines to fully connected setups. Some even feature live and on-demand classes, immersive virtual rides, and easy syncing with popular fitness platforms like Strava.

All of our editors and test team ride or train indoors for at least part of the year, sometimes even during the summer months to escape the heat. We’ve logged countless hours on stationary bikes and standard indoor trainers. In our testing, we’ve wrestled with finicky machines, endured glitchy interfaces and endless updates, and spent plenty of time grinding out virtual miles from our basements, garages, and home gyms; some of our editors have even taught spin classes.

Stationary bikes come in three main styles: Upright, recumbent, and dual-action. Upright models feel most like riding a traditional outdoor bike. Recumbent bikes offer a more reclined position, while dual-action bikes add upper-body work to the pedaling action.

Our testing and reviews focus on upright stationary bikes made by cycling-specific brands and general fitness companies. To differentiate between the two, we call models from fitness companies “exercise bikes” and those from cycling brands “indoor bikes” in this story.

Exercise bikes by fitness-oriented brands often feature a more upright riding position, multi-position handlebars with foam padding, and wide, comfort-style seats. The pedals usually have toe clips for use with running shoes.

Indoor bikes from traditional cycling brands typically mimic the body position, ride feel, and functional layout of outdoor bikes and feature dropbars, brake hoods, adjustable crank length, and narrow saddles. They usually feature high resistance for sprint workouts and virtual racing. These bikes used to be expensive, but prices have dropped over the last three years, making them a great choice for everyday indoor riders (not only hardcore enthusiasts).

The BowFlex C6 has the most capability at a reasonable price. High-quality and adjustable, this bike features Bluetooth connectivity so you can connect to apps like Peloton, Zwift, and Schwinn Trainer to join community rides and track progress.

The monitor displays time ridden, speed, mileage, heart rate, and resistance level. It doesn’t show wattage or precise RPM (it displays them on a scale). However, it does measure them, and you can see that data if you connect it to third-party training apps.

The flywheel is smooth and heavy, and you can crank the resistance up significantly through 100 incremental levels via a knob. Toe cages let you ride the C6 in regular running shoes or flip the pedals over and clip in with Shimano SPD cleats.

A great feature is the unit’s silence—you can use it day or night without waking your family. It comes with a forearm heart rate monitor and a pair of 3-pound dumbbells for light upper-body workouts while riding.

Want a more immersive experience? Check out BowFlex’s Velocore. It features a 22-inch integrated console with tons of class and entertainment streaming options, and is compatible with Zwift, Peloton, and JRNY.

If you don’t like traditional exercise bikes and want something that closely replicates the fit and feel of riding your actual bike, the Zwift Ride is an ideal solution—and the recently updated V2 model addresses issues our editors experienced with the first-gen model by adding adjustable crank length and saddle setback.

At its core, the Ride is an indoor cycling setup that eliminates the hassle of constantly mounting and unmounting your bike from a trainer or dedicating one bike solely for indoor use. The frame is exceptionally sturdy and has proven itself time and again under the stress of multiple test riders’ workouts. Paired with the reliable Kickr Core 2 trainer—our Best Overall smart trainer pick—the setup delivers a premium ride experience.

However, the real magic lies in its seamless integration with Zwift’s virtual world. You can join races, group rides, guided workouts, or explore immersive digital landscapes alongside fellow “Zwifters.” The most popular virtual cycling platform globally, Zwift succeeds by stripping away the monotony of indoor training. It gamifies the experience while offering social and competitive features that you can engage with as much—or as little—as you like.

The Schwinn IC4 is ideal if you want quick, easy access to ride metrics; you can see your data on the display—no subscription necessary. It also has a stand for your phone or tablet, USB charging for your devices, water bottle holders, and weights so everything you need is at your fingertips.

If you’re in the mood to be pumped up by a live class, Rouvy, or Zwift race, the Bluetooth option lets you jump right into third-party apps. The bike comes with a free two-month subscription to Schwinn’s platform, JRNY, which offers workout programming tailored to your preferences and over 200 virtual courses.

If you like the concept of the Zwift Ride but want an indoor bike with more adjustability and refinement, Wahoo’s Kickr Bike Shift is one of the best options. It’s essentially a stripped-down version of Wahoo’s super-premium, $4,000 Kickr Bike Pro; the Shift doesn’t include the Pro’s motor-electromagnetic resistance, gradient simulation, and some finishing details. While nifty features, they’re overkill for almost every indoor rider.

Like the Kickr Bike Pro, the Shift is quiet, super smooth, and easily adjustable to fit multiple users in a household. It also features standard bicycle component attachment. This makes it easy to replicate your outdoor bike’s fit on the Kickr Shift with your favorite saddle and handlebar. If you want the convenience and silence of an indoor bike, and a premium indoor riding setup, the Shift is the one to get.

Peloton redefined at-home fitness with its original bike—a sturdy, low-maintenance machine built to withstand years of sweaty daily rides. Its true draw, though, has always been Peloton’s vast library of on-demand and live classes, now spanning not only cycling but also running, core, and boot camp sessions. With the Peloton app, you can even take workouts on the go.

For years, the bike itself saw few changes—until the Bike+ arrived. It keeps the durable frame and quiet belt drive but adds a redesigned handlebar and a larger 23.8-inch touchscreen that rotates 360 degrees, making it easy to follow floor-based workouts. The model also features forward-facing Sonos-tuned speakers and auto-resistance that adjusts automatically to match instructor cues. Not everyone will use it, but those who do will love the convenience.

The most notable update is Peloton IQ: a built-in camera that tracks your movements, offers real-time feedback, and counts reps. There’s even a small fan above the screen for added comfort.

However, these upgrades come at a premium: the Bike+ is significantly more than the standard Peloton Bike. If you want to save $1,000, the standard Bike features solid build quality and full access to Peloton’s unmatched training ecosystem. But it doesn’t include auto-resistance, high-quality speakers, a rotating screen, Peloton IQ, a phone tray, and a fan.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike features a 35-pound flywheel and provides a smooth, quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable with a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches. Riders can also adjust the handlebar height and the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Although the Yosuda doesn’t connect to third-party sites, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned on the included single-button monitor. Below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame provides stability and durability, yet it’s easy to move thanks to the small wheels on the front edge.

If you’re spinning on a budget but want a connected experience, the Echelon EX-15 may be the stationary bike for you. This high-quality bike offers access to proprietary classes you can stream with an Echelon membership ($399.99 billed annually). Echelon’s membership isn’t limited to cycling content. The subscription offers rowing, running, strength training, yoga, and more. Enjoy workouts to music from artists including Pitbull and Lady Gaga—plus dance, EDM, hip hop, K-Pop, metal, Latin, and R&B.

The EX-15 bike itself is sized perfectly for smaller spaces, yet doesn’t skimp on comforts like an extra-large cushioned seat and padded handlebars. The mechanical knob lets you adjust resistance between 32 levels. You also get a free 30-day membership when you buy the EX-15 through Amazon.

It’s important to have one with solid construction and high weight capacity if you plan to put your stationary bike through the wringer. The Sunny Evolution Pro can withstand your most intense intervals and feels stable doing it. The 135-pound steel frame has a large footprint with leveling stabilizers in each corner to help prevent rocking.

Complementing that is a hefty 44-pound flywheel, which eliminates the inconsistent resistance you can feel near the top end of lighter wheels. The adjustable handlebar moves up and down and front to back, so you can dial in a position that's comfortable for your back, neck, and wrists.

The seat height accommodates riders with inseam lengths from 29 to 39 inches—a downside if you’re on the shorter side (Our 5-foot-2 barely made the cut, but awesome if you’re taller).

The Evolution Pro’s simplicity also makes it a great pick. Without Bluetooth connectivity (or even a monitor to display metrics), you can exercise without getting bogged down in numbers and be more in touch with your body at different PRE (perceived rate of exertion) levels.

The Keiser M3i is a studio-level spin bike with a clean, streamlined design and simplified interface. It has everything you need to nail your numbers in a hard workout, and then upload that data to apps like TrainingPeaks or Strava. The smooth flywheel is quiet, and its rear location means fewer sweat droplets land on it, so you can worry less about corrosion or wiping it down perfectly. The small monitor displays your power, cadence, time, gear, heart rate (if you’re wearing a connected strap), and total distance.

The media tray holds a phone or tablet above your handlebar so you can follow a route or guided workout as you ride, and it automatically uploads each effort in the included Keiser app to track your progress.

The saddle height adjustment uses preset stops; however, the wedge system lets you place the saddle in the precise spot you prefer. The looped handlebar is comfortable for a wide range of reaches, and the height adjustment accommodates riders as short as 4-foot-10 and as tall as 7 feet.

Stationary bikes come in three main options: upright, recumbent, and dual-action. The bikes recommended here are upright style, which puts you in a position that mimics how you’d sit on a traditional bicycle.

Recumbent exercise bikes seat you in a slightly reclined position with the pedals out in front of your hips rather than directly below, which can be easier on your back and neck. Dual-action exercise bikes have handlebars that move in and out, so riders incorporate their arms into the workout as they pedal.

Look for models with adjustable saddle height and position, plus adjustable handlebars. More adjustability makes it easier to find a comfortable riding position and get a good workout. Like a regular bicycle, a proper fit is crucial for the best experience. I like my indoor bike’s fit to match the position I ride outdoors.

All bikes feature bar-height adjustments, and some models let you adjust reach. Saddle height and setback adjustment options are also a must-have. They also have graduated markings, making it easier to get back to your preferred position after someone else uses the bike.

A dropbar offers hand positions that mimic road bikes, while a traditional bullhorn bar will be more familiar to those of you who frequent studio classes.

The two most common methods for regulating an indoor bike’s resistance are friction and magnets. Friction-based systems use leather or synthetic pads that press against a flywheel—It’s a simple, effective way to add precise, linear resistance. These resistance systems don’t require outside power to operate.

Magnetic resistance is quieter than friction systems. They use magnets (adjacent to the flywheel) to create an electric current that resists the wheel’s rotation. By increasing the current (strengthening the magnetic force), you have greater resistance. With no contact between the flywheel and magnets, this type of bike may offer a smoother ride than a friction-based one.

Some models use electromagnetic resistance controlled by software from a connected app. This allows platforms like Zwift to replicate hills and wind.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Bluetooth-equipped exercise bikes let you transmit your ride data directly to third-party training apps like Peloton or Zwift for in-ride metrics. If it has ANT+ capability, you can connect to extra sensors—like a cadence tracker or heart rate monitor—and display that data on your monitor or tablet. It’s not totally necessary for an interactive experience.

If you want to join virtual classes but aren’t sure which you’ll like (or you enjoy several), look for a bike with connectivity and media compatibility that lets you join the most platforms.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Most indoor bikes function similarly; the accessories that set them apart. The most basic models are as simple as it gets, just an ergometer with a weighted flywheel and a pad to set resistance. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes like the Peloton, with elaborate software for recorded and live classes.

Decide how much technology you actually need for your indoor rides. Some cyclists want a feature-rich experience with training plans, classes, and group rides, while others want a stripped-down bike that covers the bare essentials.

Measure your available space before buying. If you will need to move it, also check the model’s weight and whether it has wheels.

Seat comfort matters; if possible, test-ride the seat that comes with your stationary bike before buying to make sure it's comfortable for you. Most stationary bikes come with a basic, comfort-style saddle. Models that allow you to swap the seat for aftermarket options offer more flexibility.
